addition order of every output element untouched, which is why they can be fixed without
weakening the guarantee.

## What

Three independent commits.

**01 — Fuse residual RMSNorm on the batch-invariant path.** One program per row, reduction
confined to that row, so a row's result does not depend on how many rows share the launch. The
three cases that change the arithmetic rather than just the fusion (`cast_x_before_out_mul`,
`rl_on_policy_target == "fsdp"`, `variance_size_override`) still take the native path. Both

only unrolls along k. Splits are sized by K rather than counted, so the split count depends on
K alone and never on the batch, and partials reduce in a sequential loop rather than with
atomics. `BLOCK_N` / `num_warps` / `num_stages` follow the shape, and all three were shown

  changing its tile changes speed, not bits.

  would go to DeepGEMM with M ≤ cap runs that kernel instead, with one 16×64×128 tile (4 stages, 4 warps, one
  program per output tile). Everything else is unchanged, including the comparison-test path.
- A unit test checks the route against DeepGEMM and against its own M = 1 rows, with `rtol=0, atol=0`.

## Accuracy (all exact comparisons)

- **Tiles:** every Triton tile config tried gave DeepGEMM's output bit for bit: 1,764 / 1,764 configs on 7 of the
  model's runtime shapes.
- **Real weights:** 17 weights (Qwen3.8-27B's 8 bf16 linears and its DFlash2 drafter's 9), every M 1–64 plus 13
  prefill sizes, route on vs off: 0 mismatching elements.
- **Row invariance**, route on and off: every row of an M-row product equals that row's 1-row product, for M 1–64,
  65, 128, 697, 2,048 and 8,192.
- **End to end, greedy:** 24 prompts × 2 repetitions and 3 long prompts (2,183 / 31,975 / 127,735 tokens) give the
  same tokens and logprobs with the route on as with it off.

| | short | 2,183 tok | 127,735 tok |

| deterministic, route off | 17.98 tok/s | 18.02 | 15.96 |

TITLE: [Deterministic] SM120: route small-M bf16 GEMMs to a Triton tile that matches DeepGEMM bit for bit
AUTHOR: bill-h-lin

## Motivation

Under `--enable-deterministic-inference` on SM120, `matmul_persistent` sends bf16 GEMMs to DeepGEMM's
`sm120_bf16_gemm_impl`. At decode-sized M that kernel reads narrow weights at about a third of DRAM bandwidth. On
Qwen3.8-27B (one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, M = 1), the down projection (5120×17408) takes 315 µs (~570 GB/s) against
cuBLAS's 133 µs. Profiled over 100 decode steps, DeepGEMM was 96.8 % of a deterministic decode step (56.2 of
58.2 ms). That is why deterministic decode ran at 18.0 tok/s against 26.4 tok/s without determinism.

## Modifications

- The persistent Triton kernel in this file issues the same arithmetic as DeepGEMM's sm120 kernel: bf16
  `mma.sync` m16n8k16 products into one fp32 accumulator per output, K ascending, no split-K, one rounding. So
  changing its tile changes speed, not bits.
- New `SGLANG_BATCH_INVARIANT_OPS_SMALL_M_TRITON=<cap>`, default 0 (off). On SM120/121, a bf16-output GEMM that
  would go to DeepGEMM with M ≤ cap runs that kernel instead, with one 16×64×128 tile (4 stages, 4 warps, one
  program per output tile). Everything else is unchanged, including the comparison-test path.
- A unit test checks the route against DeepGEMM and against its own M = 1 rows, with `rtol=0, atol=0`.

## Accuracy (all exact comparisons)

- **Tiles:** every Triton tile config tried gave DeepGEMM's output bit for bit: 1,764 / 1,764 configs on 7 of the
  model's runtime shapes.
- **Real weights:** 17 weights (Qwen3.8-27B's 8 bf16 linears and its DFlash2 drafter's 9), every M 1–64 plus 13
  prefill sizes, route on vs off: 0 mismatching elements.
- **Row invariance**, route on and off: every row of an M-row product equals that row's 1-row product, for M 1–64,
  65, 128, 697, 2,048 and 8,192.
- **End to end, greedy:** 24 prompts × 2 repetitions and 3 long prompts (2,183 / 31,975 / 127,735 tokens) give the
  same tokens and logprobs with the route on as with it off.

## Speed (Qwen3.8-27B bf16, one RTX PRO 6000, single stream, cap 16)

| | short | 2,183 tok | 127,735 tok |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| deterministic, route off | 17.98 tok/s | 18.02 | 15.96 |
| **deterministic, route on** | **27.66** | **27.67** | **22.85** |
| non-deterministic default (reference) | 26.4 | 26.6 | 23.2 |

- With DFLASH speculation (8 draft tokens) in deterministic mode, short prompts go 85.6 → 106.6 tok/s and 128k goes
  37.0 → 42.6. These were measured on our tree, which also carries target-verify patches not in `main`.
- Prefill (M > 16) is unchanged.

TITLE: [sglang-miles] Cut deterministic inference overhead on ROCm

## Motivation

Deterministic inference (`--enable-deterministic-inference`) is much slower than the default
on ROCm. Three kernels on the batch-invariant path are responsible
1.  residual RMSNorm has no batch-invariant kernel and falls back to eager PyTorch, the deterministic .
2.  GEMM uses one fixed tile config that wastes most of its tile on decode-shaped inputs.
3. and the unified prefill attention walks the whole KV length even for query blocks whose later keys are all masked.
This PR fixes all three. **ROCm only** — no CUDA path is touched.

## Modifications

Three commits, one per kernel:

1. **Fuse residual RMSNorm.** Add a Triton kernel for
   `x, residual = rms_norm(x + residual), x + residual`, so the pattern stops falling back to
   `forward_native`, which ran the add, square, mean, rsqrt and multiply as separate launches.
4. **Autotune the deterministic GEMM while staying batch invariant.** Split the choice in two:
   the K split is sized from K alone, and BLOCK_M / BLOCK_N / num_warps / num_stages come from
   the shape plus the card's CU count and LDS size. Only the K split can move the accumulation
   order, so only it has to ignore the batch.
5. **Bound the prefill attention loop by causality.** Stop the KV loop at the causal bound. A
   dropped tile would have added `exp(-inf) = 0` to the online softmax, so the output is
   bitwise identical, not an approximation.

- With --enable-deterministic-inference and --speculative-algorithm EAGLE3 together, results changed from run to run. Without EAGLE3, they were completely stable. - It only works with three attention backends: FlashInfer, FlashAttention 3 (FA3), and Triton.
- It builds on Thinking Machines Lab's batch-invariant operators and stays compatible with chunked prefill, CUDA graphs, radix cache, and non-greedy sampling. Speculative decoding isn't on that list.
- It also works with non-greedy sampling if you set sampling seeds. The default seed is 42.
- Performance: SGLang reports an average slowdown of only 34.35% with the FlashInfer and FA3 backends, compared with the 61.5% slowdown in Thinking Machines Lab's blog.

**Roadmap**
- The deterministic inference tracking issue (#10278) lists speculative decoding among its items, next to related questions like "[Question] Speculative Decoding: Sampling from the draft probs vector #9877". That suggests the work is planned or underway, not finished.

If you need reproducible outputs, for example for RL rollouts, you'd have to turn speculative decoding off for now. You can test whether your build is deterministic with `python3 -m sglang.test.test_deterministic`. Every test should report "Unique samples: 1".

Here's what I found on vLLM batch invariance, speculative decoding, and getting bitwise-identical results between verify (prefill) and decode in 2026.

**Status of vLLM's batch-invariant mode**
- You turn it on with one environment variable, `export VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`. You can also put it in front of the server start command.
- It needs NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability 8.0 or higher.
- It is still in beta, not generally available. That note was in both the dev and stable docs as of August 23, 2026.

**Recent work on prefill and decode giving the same bits**
- vLLM PR #55627 (Mamba2): with VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1, Mamba2 layers now give the same bits for prefill, chunked prefill and decode within one process. The author is careful about how far this goes. It was measured on GB200 (SM100) with Triton 3.7.1, and other GPUs, Triton versions and shapes weren't checked, so it's "a measurement, not a guarantee."
- A correction dated September 8, 2026 found a case where it fails. With chunk size 64 and 8 heads, the dt-cumsum kernel's fp32 prefix sums change depending on the autotuned tile, and the difference shows up in the outputs.
- The same PR fixed a tensor-parallel issue. The gated RMSNorm's TP > 1 path used torch's sum, whose reduction order depends on the token count. It now reduces per-rank means instead, which made decode match prefill at TP=2.
- There's also a related NeMo RL proposal: "zero train-generation mismatch via upstream batch-invariant kernels" (NVIDIA-NeMo/RL#4039).

**Why this matters for speculative decoding**
- The Vosti paper (arXiv 2609.38981) explains the link: different logits can change which draft tokens get accepted, and they break the prefill–decode equivalence that speculative verification expects. Under speculative decoding, the same request may go through a multi-token prefill or a single-token decode.
- Vosti formally proves determinism. A Verus proof covers scheduling and the paged, prefix-sharing KV cache, and a Triton analyzer proves selected kernels give bitwise-equal outputs across batches, query lengths and KV-cache layouts. Its performance on decode-heavy workloads is comparable to vLLM's batch-invariant mode, with a stronger guarantee.
- It only claims determinism within one parallel setup. Matching bits across different GPU counts or partitionings needs extra constraints.

**Another approach: LLM-42 (arXiv 2601.17768, January 2026)**
- LLM-42 gets determinism through "verified speculation" rather than batch-invariant kernels. The authors argue batch-invariant kernels guarantee determinism but are "fundamentally over-constrained."
- Its own limitations: prefill and decode use different reduction strategies, so it isn't prefill-decode invariant. It can't share prefix caches across turns or requests, and it doesn't yet work with speculative-decoding-based inference.
- A blog post sums up the cost argument: even if only 1% of traffic needs determinism, changing the kernels slows down the other 99%.

**Related reading**
- The vLLM blog has a post on how vLLM and TorchTitan get bitwise-consistent on-policy RL by matching training and inference numerics with batch-invariant kernels.
- "Batch Speculative Decoding Done Right" (arXiv 2510.22876) covers whether batched speculative decoding is algorithmically correct, rather than bitwise determinism. It notes that neither vLLM nor SGLang supports continuous-batching speculative decoding with external draft models.

None of these sources says outright that vLLM's batch-invariant mode is officially supported together with speculative decoding. The latest vLLM docs and the batch-invariance guide are the places to check whether that combination works.

Short answer: in theory, greedy speculative decoding gives exactly the same output as normal greedy decoding. In practice it often doesn't match bit for bit. The verification pass scores several draft tokens in one batched forward pass, which does floating-point math in a different order than a one-token-at-a-time decode. That changes the logits slightly, and if the top two tokens are almost tied, the chosen token can flip.

## The theory vs. what the docs say
- Some sources say outright that for greedy decoding (temperature = 0), outputs are bit-for-bit identical. That's only true in exact math.
- vLLM's docs are more careful. They say speculative decoding is theoretically lossless up to the precision limits of hardware numerics, and that variations in generated outputs with and without speculative decoding can occur due to following factors: Floating-Point Precision. They also warn that changes in batch size may cause variations in logprobs and output probabilities, potentially due to non-deterministic behavior in batched operations or numerical instability.

## Real cases
- **omphalos (Issue #161):** Speculative (MTP) and non-speculative outputs matched up to token 47, then split. The plain decode's logits there: top-1 5604 at 27.25796, top-2 20554 at 27.25579 — a gap of 0.0022; speculation picked 20554. The cause given: the verification rows (NT = 2..4 GEMVs, multi-token attention tiles) are not bit-identical to the single-token decode step, and some arithmetic still depends on how many tokens a step runs.
- **llama.cpp (Issue #27407):** Greedy output diverges with speculation on CUDA. The divergence is deterministic (reruns are byte-identical) and is classified as CUDA numerical divergence under batched speculative verification, not a logic bug. The suspected cause is CUDA fp-non-associativity in the batched verification decode (e.g. n_max=7 draft batch in one flash-attn batch vs sequential target decode). Outputs remain coherent; this is a bit-exactness concern only. On Metal, by contrast, z-lab's Metal validation of DFlash2 achieved byte-identical greedy output, which points to a platform-specific numerics factor.
- **Production report (vLLM, Llama-3.1-8B):** A team ran the same 2,000 prompts through both paths, greedy, temperature 0. 1.2% of outputs differed. Their evals missed it because we were evaluating one numerical path and shipping another.

## Research
- **"Batch Speculative Decoding Done Right" (arXiv 2510.22876):** Their method reached 95% decoding-equivalence with residual divergence attributable to floating-point non-determinism in GPU inference, not synchronization failures. They also found that all existing implementations fail to preserve output equivalence when batch size exceeds one. That second finding is a real bug, separate from floating-point noise.
- **LLM-42 (arXiv 2601.17768):** Explains why one tiny difference grows. In practice, such boundary-crossing events are rare, as numerical drift typically perturbs logits only slightly. However, autoregressive decoding amplifies even a single such deviation: once a token differs, all subsequent tokens may diverge. It turns verification into a tool for determinism: because the input shape is fixed during verification, replayed tokens follow a consistent reduction order.

## Takeaways
1. **Floating-point noise or a real bug?** Floating-point divergence happens rarely, at near-ties, and the text stays coherent. If output is consistently worse, that points to the implementation: if your output is reproducibly worse across many prompts, that's an implementation problem.
2. **How to diagnose:** At the first token that differs, log the top-2 logit gap. A tiny gap (like the 0.0022 above) means numerics.
3. **How to fix it:** Make the kernels give the same per-row result whether they process 1 token or several (the omphalos approach). Or force verification to run tokens one at a time (asked about in llama.cpp #27407). Otherwise, document the guarantee as "identical up to floating-point near-ties."
4. **Evaluation:** Test through the same serving path you run in production, and consider a canary that compares speculative vs. non-speculative outputs.

- **"Batch Speculative Decoding Done Right" (arXiv 2510.22876):** Their method reached 95% decoding-equivalence with residual divergence attributable to floating-point non-determinism in GPU inference, not synchronization failures. They also found that all existing implementations fail to preserve output equivalence when batch size exceeds one. That second finding is a real bug, separate from floating-point noise.
- **LLM-42 (arXiv 2601.17768):** Explains why one tiny difference grows. In practice, such boundary-crossing events are rare, as numerical drift typically perturbs logits only slightly. However, autoregressive decoding amplifies even a single such deviation: once a token differs, all subsequent tokens may diverge. It turns verification into a tool for determinism: because the input shape is fixed during verification, replayed tokens follow a consistent reduction order.

## Takeaways
1. **Floating-point noise or a real bug?** Floating-point divergence happens rarely, at near-ties, and the text stays coherent. If output is consistently worse, that points to the implementation: if your output is reproducibly worse across many prompts, that's an implementation problem.
2. **How to diagnose:** At the first token that differs, log the top-2 logit gap. A tiny gap (like the 0.0022 above) means numerics.
3. **How to fix it:** Make the kernels give the same per-row result whether they process 1 token or several (the omphalos approach). Or force verification to run tokens one at a time (asked about in llama.cpp #27407). Otherwise, document the guarantee as "identical up to floating-point near-ties."
4. **Evaluation:** Test through the same serving path you run in production, and consider a canary that compares speculative vs. non-speculative outputs.

======== ggml-org/llama.cpp#27407 IS [2026-08-19] state=open comments=2 (rate rem 46)
TITLE: spec: greedy output diverges from non-speculative baseline under batched verification on CUDA (deterministic numerics; draft-simple alone reproduces, DFlash2 amplifies)
AUTHOR: indubwestep

## Summary

With speculative decoding enabled (`temp 0`, fixed seed, otherwise identical settings), greedy output diverges from the identical non-speculative run. The divergence is **deterministic** (reruns are byte-identical) and is classified as **CUDA numerical divergence under batched speculative verification**, not a logic bug: the plain `draft-simple` path — which exercises batched verification with none of the DFlash2 code — reproduces it on one workload, while the DFlash2 path amplifies it (diverges on both workloads tested, and earlier).

Outputs remain coherent; this is a bit-exactness concern only, and speculative acceptance is unaffected. No fix is claimed here — this is a documentation/confirmation request.

## Environment

- llama.cpp at PR #27342 head: `5ecbe1ac17ec0484c5b44af0bd580cdc9c428ed4` (local build, MSVC 19.44, CUDA 12.4, sm_86)
- OS: Windows 11 x86_64
- GPU: NVIDIA RTX 3090 Ti 24 GB
- Target: `empero-ai/Qwen3.8-27B-Ridge-GGUF` `Qwen3.8-27B-Ridge-3.7bpw.gguf` (IQ2_M)
- Draft: `incoai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2-GGUF` `Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2-Q4_K_M.gguf` (1,143,006,752 bytes; SHA-256 `18a380efc9b7ed8d88677fc895f5c11ae170653434ee378f7348f715c14d0594`)

## Repro (llama-cli, 6 runs)

Baseline (`--spec-type none`):

```
llama-cli -m <target> -ngl 999 --flash-attn on -c 8192 \
  --cache-type-k q4_0 --cache-type-v q4_0 -b 256 -ub 128 -t 8 \
  --temp 0 -s 42 --no-display-prompt -no-cnv -st \
  -n 256 -f prompt_short.txt < nul
```

Speculative variants add:

```
  -md <draft> --spec-draft-ngl 999 --spec-draft-n-max 7 --spec-draft-p-min 0 \
  --spec-type draft-simple        # or draft-dflash
```

Run the same with `-n 512 -f prompt_coding.txt`. Note: `--draft-model` is **not** a valid flag in this build; use `-md` (cli) / `--spec-draft-model` (server).

## Results (token-level, same-vocab `llama-tokenize`)

| workload | none vs draft-simple | none vs draft-dflash |
|---|---|---|
| short (n=256) | diverge at gen-token ~109 | diverge at gen-token ~49 |
| coding (n=512) | **identical 512/512** | diverge at gen-token ~372 |

Stripped-output MD5 (static banner/prompt-echo removed; generation content only):

| run | short | coding |
|---|---|---|
| none | `db0b78ede21fcb32543217e5cbfd437f` (1330 B) | `1d69d9619a1bde9249dac21e6fccaf99` (2482 B) |
| draft-simple | `c55e97dec9b537272f72dc578e1f00dc` (1346 B) | `1d69d9619a1bde9249dac21e6fccaf99` (2482 B) — **= none** |
| draft-dflash | `25dfca084f4cec36bc8f71f5eaa8da24` (1401 B) | `24d531f596c8aa41c1119ea01bd824d7` (2459 B) |

Reruns are byte-identical (determinism confirmed).

Example near-tie flips (short workload): `" storage of information."` vs `", recall, forgetting"`; `". Too many"` vs `"syllables. Too"`. Coding workload: digit flip `"1, 2"` vs `"8, 4"` in generated code.

## Analysis

- Batched verification alone (`draft-simple`, no DFlash hooks) perturbs CUDA target logits at near-ties: it diverges on the short workload yet is byte-identical on coding → **near-tie dependent, not systematic**.
- `draft-dflash` diverges on both workloads and earlier: DFlash2's extraction graph (`llama_set_embeddings_layer_inp` graph-output marking) amplifies the numeric shift but is **not the sole cause** (proven by the `draft-simple` divergence).
- Deterministic across reruns → consistent with CUDA fp-non-associativity in the batched verification decode (e.g. n_max=7 draft batch in one flash-attn batch vs sequential target decode) and/or graph-extraction side effects.
- Supporting data point: z-lab's Metal validation of DFlash2 achieved byte-identical greedy output (see z-lab/llama.cpp-fork#1), suggesting a platform-numeric component.

## Questions

1. Is bit-exact greedy output expected to be preserved under batched speculative verification on CUDA? (MTP presumably shows the same class of divergence.)
2. Is there a supported way to force the sequential target-decode path during verification, for bit-exact comparisons?
3. If this is accepted as generic numerics, it may be worth a short note i

--- Nihmar [2026-10-02]
Root cause and fix:

- **Cause**: the FP16 window was relative to the end of the step's batch (`p + window >= seq`). In a verification of T tokens starting at p0, row t's own decode step would read keys p0 + t - 127 .. from FP16, but the batch window starts at p0 + T - 128: the T - 1 - t oldest keys of its window came from Q8/Q4. Verification rows differed from the decode step by up to ~5e-3 in the logits (bisected: `OMPH_KV_WINDOW=0` and `OMPH_KV_F32=1` make them bit-exact; GEMV NT variants and the delta-net path were not involved).
- **Alternatives**: (a) re-derive the window per query in a separate pass over the edge keys — a correction term changes the fma order, not bit-exact; (b) document "identical up to near-ties" — rejected, the identity is cheap to get; (c) chosen: the per-query rule `key >= q - window + 1` in the scalar kernel, with the ring holding `window + 15` positions (+0.94 MiB VRAM over 16 layers) so every query of a chunk of up to 16 tokens finds its whole window; the at most nt - 1 window-edge keys of a tile are read in both versions (Q8 K reloaded into the same registers for the later rows, Q8 V staged in a small LDS array). T = 1 (decode) gets the same rule it had; the WMMA prefill (T >= 16) keeps the chunk-relative window. `#pragma unroll 1` on the edge accumulation keeps the TQ = 4 kernel's scratch at 24 B (it had spilled 928 B).
- **Results** (`bench/results/spec-ring-161.txt`): 119 / 119 verification rows bit-exact against the decode step; the 2001-token / 300-token case now identical; specval.sh and an `OMPH_SPEC_CHECK` MTP run identical; main's outputs unchanged (ident.sh 6/6); speculative 19.17 -> 19.21 ms/token (+0.2 %), plain unchanged.

#136 [2026-10-01] perf: decode / verification attention at long context (fixed key chunks, shared KV reads)
Milestone: decode speed (priority 2), PLAN.md §10.4 / §12 (speculative decoding).

## Measured (main 4bc9a42)
- Decode step at 16k context: 52.6 ms vs 45.8 at 512. rocprofv3 (no overlap): `attention_gqa_kernel<true,1>` 7.27 ms/step for ~440 MB of Q8/Q4 KV, ~60 GB/s (5x under bandwidth). It grows linearly with the context.
- Speculative decoding (`--draft-mtp 3`) at 16k: 35.3 ms/token (17.5 at 512). Verification 78 ms per cycle vs 54: tokens < 8 use one-token tiles, so each verified token re-reads the whole KV.

## Plan
1. Split the keys into fixed chunks (per run, from the context capacity) instead of a per-call split count. Every query then sums its keys in the same order in any call, so speculative greedy equals plain greedy exactly. #97's fix covered the batch-size dependence but not a batch that straddles a 16-key block boundary.
2. Verifications share each KV read across their tokens (tiles of 2-4 tokens). The per-row arithmetic does not depend on the tile size: bit-identical to one-token decode.
3. Kernel efficiency: DPP row reductions instead of `ds_bpermute`, 16-byte V loads staged through LDS.

Done = decode step and speculative ms/token at 512 / 16k before/after, spec oracle runs identical in every KV mode, KL vs the exact f32 KV unchanged.

The `draft-dflash` arms are PR #27342 at `d1a522f` and are compared only against a no-speculation baseline built from that same branch.

The divergence reproduces and is deterministic, as you found. 76 to 80 % of requests differ from their baseline depending on the arm, forking at a median 23 % into the text, and every arm is byte-identical to itself across all five passes.

What might be worth following is that the fork position is a function of verification width. Running `n_max` 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7, so widths 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8, the character index of the first difference is **identical inside two groups and different between them**: widths 3 and 4 agree on 25 of 25 prompts, widths 5, 6 and 8 agree on 25 of 25, and the two groups land somewhere different on 14 of them. Same structure in all five passes. The grouping crosses drafter types, so `draft-mtp` at width 6 sits with `draft-dflash` at widths 5 and 8 rather than with the other `draft-mtp` arms.

- **Results** (`bench/results/spec-ring-161.txt`): 119 / 119 verification rows bit-exact against the decode step; the 2001-token / 300-token case now identical; specval.sh and an `OMPH_SPEC_CHECK` MTP run identical; main's outputs unchanged (ident.sh 6/6); speculative 19.17 -> 19.21 ms/token (+0.2 %), plain unchanged.

#136 [2026-10-01] perf: decode / verification attention at long context (fixed key chunks, shared KV reads)
Milestone: decode speed (priority 2), PLAN.md §10.4 / §12 (speculative decoding).

## Measured (main 4bc9a42)
- Decode step at 16k context: 52.6 ms vs 45.8 at 512. rocprofv3 (no overlap): `attention_gqa_kernel<true,1>` 7.27 ms/step for ~440 MB of Q8/Q4 KV, ~60 GB/s (5x under bandwidth). It grows linearly with the context.
- Speculative decoding (`--draft-mtp 3`) at 16k: 35.3 ms/token (17.5 at 512). Verification 78 ms per cycle vs 54: tokens < 8 use one-token tiles, so each verified token re-reads the whole KV.

## Plan
1. Split the keys into fixed chunks (per run, from the context capacity) instead of a per-call split count. Every query then sums its keys in the same order in any call, so speculative greedy equals plain greedy exactly. #97's fix covered the batch-size dependence but not a batch that straddles a 16-key block boundary.
2. Verifications share each KV read across their tokens (tiles of 2-4 tokens). The per-row arithmetic does not depend on the tile size: bit-identical to one-token decode.
3. Kernel efficiency: DPP row reductions instead of `ds_bpermute`, 16-byte V loads staged through LDS.

# vLLM Batch Invariance: Extracted Details

## Hardware support
- **NVIDIA:** "NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability 8.0 or higher."
- **Intel XPU:** "Intel XPUs with Triton support." The page also says "On XPU, Triton Attention backend is required for batch invariance."
- **AMD ROCm:** The page does not list it as a supported platform. AMD tech appears only in the list of things that get turned off: it "disables FlashInfer, AITER and QuickReduce all-reduce."

## What is guaranteed
- The feature "ensures that the output of a model is deterministic and independent of the batch size" and also of "the order of requests in a batch."
- The feature is labeled beta: "Batch invariance is currently in beta."
- Validation covers only listed models: "Other models may also work, but these have been explicitly validated."
- There is a TP caveat: invariance "is not yet supported for all-reduces whose size isn't a multiple of 16 bytes." Such tensors "can switch between NCCL and custom all-reduce depending on batch size." The page adds that "All validated models meet this requirement."

## Speculative decoding
The page doesn't address it at all, so it is neither confirmed as supported nor stated as excluded.

## Performance overhead
- The page gives no numbers, only a qualitative note: "Enabling batch invariance may impact performance compared to the default non-deterministic mode."
- It frames the cost as deliberate: "This trade-off is intentional to guarantee reproducibility."

## Implementation details
- **Kernels:** "Uses deterministic kernel implementations for attention and other operations."
- **Disabled features:** It turns off "sequence parallelism / async TP, whose reduce-scatter path is not batch-invariant."
- **All-reduce under TP:** Custom all-reduce stays on with a fixed order: "the 1-stage kernel is pinned, and large inputs are reduced in fixed-size chunks."
- **Matmul on CUDA (Ada, Hopper, Blackwell):** It "runs without `torch.compile` using breakable CUDA graphs so tile configs follow the runtime batch size." You can opt out with `VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH=0`.
- **LoRA:** "Splits the LoRA shrink reduction into 8 fixed K chunks that are summed in a fixed order instead of with atomics."
- **Not mentioned:** persistent matmul, split-KV strategy, and general split-K choices. The only K-splitting described is the LoRA one above.
- **Attention backends:** The only one named is TRITON_ATTN, which is required on XPU. No NVIDIA attention backend is specified.

## Prefill/decode consistency and query-length invariance
The page says nothing about either. Its stated scope covers only batch size and request order.

## Speculative Decoding in vLLM on AMD GPUs: Summary

**AMD GPUs**
- The tests ran on AMD Instinct MI300X and MI355X with ROCm.
- The visible text does not say which experiments ran on which GPU. The page is truncated near the end.
- Tensor parallelism was TP=2 for most models and TP=4 for Qwen3.5-122B. Qwen3-8B appears to run on a single GPU.

**Methods tested**
- Native MTP (Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6)
- Gemma 4 MTP, using a separate assistant checkpoint that shares the target KV cache
- EAGLE-3 (autoregressive drafter using fused early, middle and late hidden states)
- DFlash (parallel block drafting with an anchor token)
- DSpark (DFlash backbone plus a lightweight Markov head)

For DSpark, the confidence head that picks a shorter prefix "was not active in the vLLM path used for our experiments."

**Measured speedups (output throughput vs. non-speculative baseline)**

| Model | Results |
|---|---|
| gemma-4-26B-A4B | DFlash up to 2.87× (MATH500, N=7); Gemma 4 MTP up to 2.83× (MATH500, N=5); EAGLE-3 2.11–2.27× |
| gemma-4-31B | DFlash 2.34× (MATH500); Gemma 4 MTP 2.00–2.20×; DSpark up to 2.20× |
| Qwen3-8B | DSpark 1.15–1.63×; DFlash 1.08–1.27×; EAGLE-3 below baseline on MATH500 (max 0.88×, 0.44× at N=1) |
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B | Native MTP 2.20× (MATH500, N=7), better than DFlash |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | DFlash 1.77–2.06× (N=7); MTP 1.28–1.49×, with N=1 below baseline (~0.87–0.89×) |
| Kimi-K2.5 | EAGLE-3 up to 2.33×; DFlash up to 2.68× |
| MiniMax-M3-MXFP8 | EAGLE-3 2.09× (HumanEval, N=4) |

- The best proposal length varied by model and workload.
- For DFlash and DSpark, N=7 was often among the fastest settings. Large N sometimes fell below 1× (e.g., Qwen3.5-122B DFlash at N=15: 0.94–0.95×).

**Verification cost, skinny GEMM, wvSplitK, kernel choice**
- There is no discussion of skinny GEMM, wvSplitK, or GEMM kernel selection for multi-token verification.
- Verification cost is only treated generically: throughput depends on "whether the saved target-model decoding work outweighs the cost of drafting and verification."
- The only kernel-related choice shown is in the serve commands: DFlash and DSpark runs use `--attention-backend triton_attn`, and some runs set `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1`. Neither choice is explained.

**Output equality, losslessness, determinism**
- Losslessness is asserted conceptually, not tested. The post says multiple tokens are committed "while preserving the target model's output behavior."
- "Model quality relative to the non-speculative baseline" is listed as an indicator, but the visible content reports no quality or equality results.
- Determinism and bit-exactness are not discussed.

**Batch invariance**
- Not discussed.
- Concurrency and batch-size effects are listed as future work: "Broader evaluation across concurrency levels, prompt and output lengths, batch sizes…"

The page has a "Lossless guarantees of Speculative Decoding" section, but I can only quote short excerpts of 125 characters or fewer, so below is a summary with brief quotes rather than the full verbatim text.

**Three areas of guarantees:**

1. **Theoretical losslessness:** Sampling is "theoretically lossless up to the precision limits of hardware numerics." The docs add that "Floating-point errors might cause slight variations in output distributions."
2. **Algorithmic losslessness:** The implementation is "algorithmically validated to be lossless." Two tests support this:
   - *Rejection Sampler Convergence* checks that the sampler's outputs "align with the target distribution."
   - *Greedy Sampling Equality* checks that greedy output with speculation "matches greedy sampling without it."
3. **Logprob stability:** "vLLM does not currently guarantee stable token log probabilities (logprobs)." As a result, the same request can produce different outputs across runs.

**Why outputs can differ with vs. without speculation:**

- **Floating-point precision:** "Differences in hardware numerical precision may lead to slight discrepancies in the output distribution."
- **Batch size:** "Changes in batch size may cause variations in logprobs and output probabilities." The suspected causes are non-deterministic batched operations or numerical instability.

For mitigations, the page points to the FAQ entry "Can the output of a prompt vary across runs in vLLM?"

**Batch invariance:** The page never uses this term. Its only related content is the batch-size point above.

**ROCm/AMD support per method:** The page doesn't mention ROCm, AMD, or any hardware-specific support for individual methods.

# SGLang Deterministic Inference: Key Details

## Overhead of Deterministic Mode

End-to-end latency on Qwen3-8B, TP1, H200, 256 requests:

| Backend | 1024/1024 | 4096/4096 | 8192/8192 |
|---|---|---|---|
| FlashInfer | +42.6% | +46.0% | +24.4% |

**1) Why matmul batch invariance breaks, and the cost of fixing it**
- Split-K: "Splitting along the reduction dimension in a matmul is known as a Split-K Matmul." The post adds, "just like RMSNorm, using this strategy breaks batch invariance."
- When it's needed: "split-k is most needed when **both** M and N are small." For LLMs, "N (i.e. the model dim) is usually pretty large!"
- Tensor-core instructions: each one "may have a different reduction order internally." With a small batch, a big instruction wastes compute, and "At a batch-size of 1, the fastest kernels usually don't use tensor cores at all."
- Tile sizes: a "jigsaw" pattern comes from "quantization effects (both tile and wave)" that are "typically ameliorated through changing tile sizes."
- Fix: "compile one kernel configuration and use that for all shapes."
- Cost: "we only lose about 20% performance compared to cuBLAS," and the kernel is described as "not an optimized Triton kernel either (e.g. no TMA)."

**2) Attention**
- Attention has to handle "inference optimizations that affect how sequences get processed (chunked prefill, prefix caching, etc.)."
- Numerics must be "invariant to both how many requests are processed at once and how each request gets sliced up."
- Requirement: the "reduction order for a given token does not depend on how many other tokens from its sequence" are in flight.
- Fix for the KV cache: "update the KV cache and page table before the attention kernel itself."
- Split-KV: "it's not sufficient to choose a fixed number of splits regardless of the batch size." Instead, "we must adopt a 'fixed split-size' strategy."
- How it works: "we fix the size of each split and then end up with a varying number of splits." For example, a KV length of 1000 becomes "three fixed-size length 256 splits and one length 232 split."
- FlashInfer, by contrast, "chooses the largest split-size that can still saturate all the GPU's cores."
- Caveat: this "requires some internal FlexAttention changes that are not included in our code release."

**3) End-to-end timing**
- Setup: "one GPU running Qwen-3-8B, and request 1000 sequences with an output length of between 90 and 110."
- Results from the table:
  - vLLM default: 26 s
  - Unoptimized Deterministic vLLM: 55 s
  - With the improved attention kernel: 42 s
- Explanation: "the FlexAttention integration in vLLM has not been heavily optimized yet."

**4) Speculative decoding**
- The article doesn't mention it.

**5) Date and author**
- Written by Horace He "in collaboration with others at Thinking Machines," dated Sep 10, 2025.

# Vosti: Verified Deterministic LLM Inference (Duke, arXiv 2609.38981)

## 1. Determinism specification
- **Definition:** With a fixed model and deployment configuration W, two requests that share a prompt and initial sampler state must yield "bitwise-identical logits at corresponding output positions across executions."
- **Prefix-comparable views:** Each request's output history must be prefix-comparable with the other. Where both executions reach an output index, the logit bits and tokens must match.
- **What it abstracts away:** The spec looks only at observable outputs. It makes no assumption about batching, chunking or the presence of a KV-cache.
- **Variations covered:**
  - batch composition and order
  - chunked-prefill budgets
  - prefill vs. decode
  - prefix reuse and KV eviction/recompute
  - query lengths and paged KV layouts
- **Engine theorem (Verus):** Each step's logits equal Forward(W, history), defined as a cold forward pass from an empty cache.
- **What it does not guarantee:**
  - It is "not a liveness property."
  - It is not functional correctness.
  - It says nothing about agreement across dtypes, compilers or hardware.

## 2. Kernels and how they are chosen
- **Kernel set:** All kernels are Triton (attention with full and sliding-window variants, linear/matmul, normalization, activation), compiled by the unmodified Triton compiler.
- **Fixed configuration:** At initialization, the engine fixes kernel specializations and tile parameters based on the model and deployment. They do not depend on batch size, chunk size, or whether a request is prefilling or decoding.
- **No fallback:** There is no runtime autotuning. A missing configuration is rejected.
- **Matmul tiles:** Tile sizes depend on N and K, not the runtime M.
- **Kernel verification:** A Z3-based analyzer checks Triton annotations to prove "bitwise-equal selected kernel outputs across batches, query lengths, and paged KV-cache layouts."
- **Not yet supported:** Dispatching among multiple bitwise-equivalent kernels is listed as future work.

## 3. Speculative decoding
- It appears mainly as motivation: differing logits can "violate the prefill–decode equivalence expected by speculative verification."
- Vosti tests prefill–decode equivalence (384 pairs per model). However, the paper does not list speculative decoding among the engine's implemented features (continuous batching, chunked prefill, prefix caching).

## 4. Failures in production deterministic modes
Versions tested: vLLM 0.28.0 and SGLang 0.5.19, on Llama3.1-8B and Gemma3-4B.

**Llama3.1-8B**
- vLLM batch-invariant (both backends) and SGLang deterministic FA3 matched every pair.
- SGLang deterministic Triton failed on prefill–decode (3/384) and prefix reuse (13/14).

**Gemma3-4B** (every production deterministic configuration failed in every category)

| Config | Batch | Chunk | P–D | Prefix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vLLM Inv. FA3 | 193/296 | 0/90 | 5/384 | 11/14 |
| vLLM Inv. Triton | 242/296 | 0/90 | 192/384 | 13/14 |
| SGLang Det. FA3 | 206/296 | 70/90 | 5/384 | 10/14 |
| SGLang Det. Triton | 256/296 | 70/90 | 3/384 | 9/14 |

**Causes identified:**
- **FA3 (both engines):** A batch-wide K-length bound decides whether local-window masking is needed, which changes specialization and tiling.
- **SGLang decode graphs:** Wider KV page tables change a similar specialization decision.
- **SGLang Triton:** Prefill and decode use different numerical algorithms.
- **vLLM invariant Triton:** Query partitioning changes which fully masked tiles are visited, and a running maximum of −∞ can be replaced by zero.

The authors frame these as scope limits, not necessarily bugs.

## 5. Performance
- **vs. vLLM batch-invariant:**
  - Decode throughput is "1.36–3.19×" higher.
  - Synthetic agentic sessions complete "1.14–2.20×" faster.
  - Prefill throughput is lower.
- **vs. default (non-deterministic) vLLM and SGLang deterministic:** Vosti is slower. No specific ratio is quoted.
- **Why:** Vosti uses smaller matmul tiles, which favor decode, while vLLM's larger tiles favor prefill.
- **Session workload:** Decode accounts for 91–93% of Vosti's session time.
- **Determinism results:** Vosti passes all "5,488 bitwise comparisons" (784 per model).

## 6. Hardware and models
- **GPU:** A single NVIDIA H200 (H200 NVL for performance runs). Only one GPU is supported. There is no AMD GPU.
- **Verification machine:** Two AMD EPYC 9355 CPUs (verification only).
- **Precision:** BF16.
- **Models:** Llama3.1-8B, Llama3.2-3B, Gemma3-4B, Gemma3-12B, Gemma3-27B, Gemma4-12B, Gemma4-31B.
- **Not yet supported:** MoE, linear attention and multi-GPU are discussed as future work.

# CoRun (arXiv 2608.14376): Extracted Specifics

## (1) Position invariance: definition and evidence
- **Definition 2:** a kernel is position-invariant if it is "equivariant to permutations at a fixed shape," meaning Fₙ(PX) = PFₙ(X).
- **Contrast with batch invariance:** batch invariance requires identical output across any batch size, co-runners, or slot. Position invariance holds only when the shape stays fixed. "Batch invariance implies position invariance, but the converse does not hold."
- **Evidence (Table I):**
  - Not batch-invariant but position-invariant: Mean, RMSNorm, SoftMax, MatMul.
  - Neither property: Ring AllReduce and FlashAttention with Split-KV.
  - Both properties: Fixed-Tree AllReduce and FlashAttention without Split-KV.
- **Source of the verification:** the authors cite prior work (LLM-42, Thinking Machines) for the "shape-consistent reduction" behavior. They state every kernel exercised "has been verified to be position-invariant or batch-invariant," citing LLM-42 rather than presenting a new verification.

## (2) Mechanism
- **Isolated prefill:**
  - Each prompt is prefilled alone (batch size 1) at its natural length, with no global padding.
  - It is built as a wrapper around the vLLM scheduler (Algorithms 1–2).
  - Prefill-time Split-KV stays enabled, since a request's prefill shape never varies.
  - A waiting request is admitted only if KV capacity can hold its full configured sequence. This avoids preemption and recomputation.
- **Fixed-shape decode:**
  - Every decode step is padded to max_num_reqs. The configuration is `cudagraph_mode=full_decode_only`, `--cudagraph-capture-sizes 256`, `--max-num-reqs 256`.
  - Exactly one CUDA graph is captured and replayed. Unused slots hold masked padding tokens.
  - Split-KV is turned off for decode, and collectives use a fixed reduction tree.
  - No changes were made to the model runner or the CUDA graph code.
- **Sampling:**
  - The sampler input is also padded to max_num_reqs, because sampling runs outside the graph.
  - RNG state is tied to the request rather than the batch slot, and padding entries never consume it.
- **What the "reference output" is:**
  - The guarantee is self-consistency within one configuration: Y is identical regardless of co-runners, slot, and arrival order.
  - It is **not** equivalent to unpadded batch-1 decoding or to STD output. Even a lone request decodes in the padded 256-slot shape.
  - The validation compares each prompt run alone against the same prompt in a batch of 32, both under CoRun. Setup: 32 prompts, temperature 0.6, seed 42, up to 8 tokens. All passed, with identical sequences and log-probs.
- **Formal argument:** determinism is argued by induction, with prefill as the base case and decode steps as the inductive step.

## (3) Measured costs
**Versus batch-invariant (BI) kernels:**
- Throughput is "15–324%" higher, and aggregate throughput "more than doubles for every evaluated model."
- Mean TTFT is 51.8% lower and mean TPOT 48.6% lower (Hy3, six workloads).
- One variable-length decode step (batch 32): STD 19.4 ms, BI 88.4 ms, CoRun 32.6 ms.
- Operator-level BI overhead:
  - Mean, RMSNorm, and Softmax are 2.12–5.61× slower.
  - MatMul is up to 36.2× slower.
  - On Qwen3-235B, MatMul groups add 8.61–19.16 ms each and attention adds 13.97 ms.
- BI reduces serving throughput by up to 74%.

**Versus the non-deterministic baseline (STD):**
- On BurstGPT with Qwen3-235B:
  - STD finishes prefill in 20 s and decode in 37 s.
  - BI takes about 40 s and 124 s.
  - CoRun does no decode during the first 30 s, then reaches 83% of STD's peak decode throughput.
- On DeepSeek-V3 (in=4096, out=128), CoRun beats STD. STD's mixed prefill/decode batches cannot use CUDA graphs with the FLASH_ATTN_MLA backend.
- **Ablations:**
  - Disabling decode Split-KV costs 15–41% with varied prompt lengths and 1–9% with similar lengths.
  - Isolated prefill is the largest source of the gap to STD.
  - With a single active request, CoRun falls below BI once padding exceeds 64.

## (4) Hardware and models
- **GPU vendor and model:** not stated anywhere (no NVIDIA/AMD SKU). CUDA graphs imply NVIDIA, but the paper does not say so.
- **Software:** vLLM 0.25.0.
- **Models:** Qwen3-235B-A22B, DeepSeek-V3, and Hy3. The LLM-42 comparison also uses Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, and Qwen3-30B-A3B.
- **Workloads:** BurstGPT, Blazedit, synthetic fixed-length workloads, and ShareGPT; 300 requests per workload.

## (5) Speculation, verification, chunked prefill
- **Speculation:** CoRun itself does no speculative decoding. It "does not generate unverified tokens, invoke a separate verifier, or roll back."
- **Comparison with LLM-42** (verified speculation, 64-token window):
  - At concurrency 256, about 4 requests become verification-eligible per iteration.
  - When 100% of traffic needs determinism, LLM-42 trails both CoRun and BI.
  - At low deterministic fractions, it can match or exceed CoRun.
  - Rollback ratios: 17.94% (Qwen3-8B), 24.25% (32B), 45.41% (30B-A3B MoE). The authors attribute the MoE result plausibly to router perturbations changing which experts are selected.
- **MarginGate** is mentioned briefly as related work.
- **Chunked prefill:**
  - Sarathi-style mixing of prefill and decode is removed.
  - A chunked long prompt continues its chunk sequence in isolation before new requests are admitted.

- **No cross-configuration reproducibility:** the guarantee does not extend across hardware, kernel versions, numeric formats, or TP degrees.

- **Sparse deterministic traffic:** when only a small fraction of requests need determinism, LLM-42 may be the better choice.
- **Proposed future work:** batch-invariant kernels for batched prefill, and prefill/decode disaggregation.

# CoRun (arXiv 2608.14376): Extracted Specifics

## (1) Position invariance: definition and evidence
- **Definition 2:** a kernel is position-invariant if it is "equivariant to permutations at a fixed shape," meaning Fₙ(PX) = PFₙ(X).
- **Contrast with batch invariance:** batch invariance requires identical output across any batch size, co-runners, or slot. Position invariance holds only when the shape stays fixed. "Batch invariance implies position invariance, but the converse does not hold."
- **Evidence (Table I):**
  - Not batch-invariant but position-invariant: Mean, RMSNorm, SoftMax, MatMul.
  - Neither property: Ring AllReduce and FlashAttention with Split-KV.
  - Both properties: Fixed-Tree AllReduce and FlashAttention without Split-KV.
- **Source of the verification:** the authors cite prior work (LLM-42, Thinking Machines) for the "shape-consistent reduction" behavior. They state every kernel exercised "has been verified to be position-invariant or batch-invariant," citing LLM-42 rather than presenting a new verification.

## (2) Mechanism
- **Isolated prefill:**
  - Each prompt is prefilled alone (batch size 1) at its natural length, with no global padding.
  - It is built as a wrapper around the vLLM scheduler (Algorithms 1–2).
  - Prefill-time Split-KV stays enabled, since a request's prefill shape never varies.
  - A waiting request is admitted only if KV capacity can hold its full configured sequence. This avoids preemption and recomputation.
- **Fixed-shape decode:**
  - Every decode step is padded to max_num_reqs. The configuration is `cudagraph_mode=full_decode_only`, `--cudagraph-capture-sizes 256`, `--max-num-reqs 256`.
  - Exactly one CUDA graph is captured and replayed. Unused slots hold masked padding tokens.
  - Split-KV is turned off for decode, and collectives use a fixed reduction tree.
  - No changes were made to the model runner or the CUDA graph code.
- **Sampling:**
  - The sampler input is also padded to max_num_reqs, because sampling runs outside the graph.
  - RNG state is tied to the request rather than the batch slot, and padding entries never consume it.
- **What the "reference output" is:**
  - The guarantee is self-consistency within one configuration: Y is identical regardless of co-runners, slot, and arrival order.

# LLM-42 (arXiv:2601.17768v2): key specifics

## 1. Mechanism (decode–verify–rollback)

**Fast path.** Requests are decoded with normal dynamic batching and the usual optimized kernels. The output is "largely—but not provably—consistent across runs."

**Verifier.** It replays a fixed-size window of recent tokens. The "fixed shape" is simply a fixed token count T per verification pass. The paper's example is "verifying 10 tokens at a time." When a sequence ends before T tokens remain, it is padded "with dummy tokens so that the verifier always processes exactly T tokens."

**Window sizes:**
- Figure 8 uses a 4-token illustration.
- Table 1 claims "longer speculation (32-64 tokens)," compared with 2–8 tokens for classic speculative decoding.
- Grouped verification batches fixed windows from several requests, e.g. "8 requests, 32 tokens each."
- Table 4 uses "8 requests, 64 tokens each."
- In the ablation, the best configurations verify 256 tokens per step, split across 16, 8, or 4 requests, giving P99 latency of 34–35 s.

**Commit rule:**
- The matching prefix is kept, plus the verifier's next token.
- Mismatched tokens after that point are discarded and the KV cache is truncated.
- Decode-phase KV entries are overwritten with the verifier's entries.
- Each verification pass yields at least one consistent token, which guarantees forward progress.

**Attention.** The verify pass uses FlashAttention-3 with KV splits set to one. Fast-path decode keeps default settings.

## 2. Shape-consistent / position-invariant observation (O2)

Kernels "apply the same reduction strategy to all elements within a given batch," and that strategy changes only when the input shape changes. Position-invariant means a token's output does not depend on its position in the batch, as long as the total batch size is fixed. The caveat is that this does not hold for kernels using atomic reductions, which the forward pass reportedly avoids.

Table 2 (batch-invariant / position-invariant):

| Operator | Batch-invariant | Position-invariant |
|---|---|---|
| cuBLAS GEMM | ✗ | ✓ |
| FA-3 (num_splits=1) | ✓ | ✓ |
| Multimem AllReduce (CUDA 13.0+) | ✓ | ✓ |
| Tree AllReduce (specific NCCL settings) | ✓ | ✓ |
| Ring AllReduce | ✗ | ✗ |
| RMSNorm and fused RMSNorm+residual | ✗ | ✓ |

## 3. What the deterministic reference output is

The committed output is the verifier's fixed-shape pass, not plain unbatched decoding. Prefill is made deterministic separately by "avoiding arbitrary batching of prefill tokens."

Batch-size-1 runs served only as "ground-truth" for the divergence study (O1). Since prefill and decode use different reduction strategies, the system is non-prefill-decode invariant. My inference is that LLM-42 output is reproducible across its own runs, but the paper does not claim it is bit-equal to unbatched decoding.

## 4. Overheads and throughput

**Kernel microbenchmarks:**
- GEMM: cuBLAS reaches 527 TFLOPS versus 194 TFLOPS for the batch-invariant Triton kernel, a 63% slowdown.
- RMSNorm: the batch-invariant Python version is up to 7× slower, and the Triton version up to 50% slower, than the non-batch-invariant CUDA kernel.

**Decode throughput (Figure 5):**

| Scenario | Tokens/s |
|---|---|
| 10 requests, non-deterministic | 845 |
| 11 requests, non-deterministic | 931 |
| SGLang-Det, 1 of 11 deterministic | ~415 (−56%) |
| LLM-42, 1 of 11 deterministic | 911 (2.2× SGLang-Det, within 3% of non-det) |

**Offline:**
- SGLang deterministic mode costs 24% (in=2048, out=512) to 36% (ShareGPT).
- At 100% deterministic traffic, LLM-42 beats SGLang-Det everywhere except ShareGPT, where it is 6% slower.
- On ArXiv, LLM-42 is within 8%, 2%, 1%, and 1% of non-det at 5%, 10%, 20%, and 50% deterministic traffic.
- LLM-42 is up to 41% faster than SGLang-Det on ArXiv in these regimes.
- At 10% deterministic traffic it is 33% faster on ShareGPT and up to 48% faster (in=2048, out=256).
- Worst case is ArXiv at 100% deterministic: 3351 rollbacks over 4096 requests and 10.97% recomputed tokens.

**Window trade-off:**
- Verification cost falls from up to 0.75 ms/token to 0.05 ms/token at window 512 (15× lower).
- Recompute overhead is 6.81% at window 32 and 46.41% at window 256.

**Online (ShareGPT):**

| Load | System | P50 | P99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12 QPS | SGLang-Det | 4.64 s | 28 s |
| 12 QPS | SGLang non-det | 2.15 s | 13.2 s |
| 12 QPS | LLM-42 @2% | 2.21 s | — |
| 18 QPS | SGLang-Det | 10.6 s | 71.1 s |
| 18 QPS | SGLang non-det | 2.84 s | 17.4 s |

- P90 TTFT at 18 QPS: 101.2 ms for LLM-42 at 100% deterministic versus 171.6 ms for SGLang-Det.
- At low QPS with 100% deterministic traffic, LLM-42 has higher latency than SGLang-Det.

**vLLM:** described only as also using batch-invariance; it is not benchmarked.

## 5. Hardware and setup

- Four NVIDIA H100 PCIe GPUs (80 GB HBM3, 114 SMs each).
- 64-core host CPU with about 1.65 TB DRAM.
- Built on SGLang 0.5.3rc0; performance results use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
- Correctness only was checked on Qwen models and on 1–4 GPUs with tensor parallelism.
- The setup has no multimem/NVLS and only pairwise NVLink, so multi-GPU performance was not evaluated.

## 6. Limitations

- Verification "induces a global pause" that stalls every in-flight request.
- Prefill is not batched in the prototype.
- The system is not prefill-decode invariant, so prefix caches cannot be shared across turns or across requests.
- It does not integrate with speculative-decoding-based inference.
- Recompute is higher online (often more than 6%) than offline (typically below 2%), because batch sizes vary more.

## 7. Venue

None stated. It is an arXiv preprint (cs.LG, v2, 30 Jan 2026) from Microsoft Research and the University of Washington. Code is promised at github.com/microsoft/llm-42.

## 1. Method, engine, hardware
- **Method:** Orthrus, a hybrid autoregressive-diffusion design. It does "self-drafting and self-verification within a frozen autoregressive backbone" (Qwen3-1.7B).
- **Models compared:**
  - The released checkpoint `chiennv/Orthrus-Qwen3-1.7B`, run with block_size 32.
  - The authors' own retrained `Orthrus-1.7B-final`, run with block_size 8. It was trained on about 4.7M greedy-distilled samples using 8×H100.
- **Inference setup:** HF Transformers `generate()` (v5.8.1), PyTorch 2.8.0+cu128, CUDA 12.8, `attn_implementation="eager"`.
- **Hardware:** a single RTX 3090 (23 GB, compute capability 8.6).

## 2. Match rates and how they were measured
- **Prompts:** 1,190 across 12 domains (100 each; gec-en has 90).
- **Decoding:** greedy, `max_new_tokens=128`, `do_sample=False`.
- **Match definition:** a trajectory matches only if it has the same length and identical token indices as the reference.

| Precision | Released checkpoint | Retrained model |
|---|---|---|
| BF16 | 0.45 [0.42, 0.48] | 0.43 [0.40, 0.46] |
| FP16 | 0.87 [0.85, 0.89] | 0.87 [0.85, 0.89] |
| FP32 | 1.00 [0.997, 1.000] | 1.00 [0.997, 1.000] |

Brackets are 95% Wilson intervals.

- **BF16 by domain:** match rates range from 0.08 (poetry-en, retrained model) to 0.88 (gec-en).
- **Tokens per forward pass:** for example, math is 8.08 (released) vs 4.99 (retrained). The retrained model is higher in 10 of 12 domains.

## 3. Why divergence happens
The paper gives only a general explanation: "discrete token selection can amplify small numerical differences into divergent generation trajectories." The authors attribute it to finite precision "without attributing it to any particular layer or computational operation."

The paper does not analyze:
- differences between the verify and decode numerical paths,
- how tokens-per-forward relates to divergence,
- specific kernels.

**Correlate found:** divergence tracks the reference model's perplexity on the response.
- BF16 mean perplexity is 1.11 for matching vs 1.28 for diverging trajectories.
- In a logistic regression controlling for response length and domain, the log-perplexity coefficient is:
  - BF16: −8.10 (released) and −10.92 (retrained), with p ≤ 3×10⁻¹¹.
  - FP16: −3.93 and −3.78, with p < 0.01.

## 4. Cost of FP32
Not reported. The paper gives no speed or memory figures for FP32, and FP32 was used only for trajectory matching, not benchmarks.

## 5. Fixes other than FP32
None proposed. Localizing the responsible operation is listed as future work. Invariant kernels are not mentioned.

## 6. Related work on determinism
The only reproducibility citation is Yuan et al. (NeurIPS 2025), which shows that precision and system configuration "can alter outputs even under greedy decoding." No batch-invariance work is cited. Speculative-decoding citations include Leviathan et al. (2023), Draft&Verify, LayerSkip, Medusa, EAGLE, Gloeckle et al. (multi-token prediction), and DeepSeek-V3.

## 7. Downstream impact
Evaluation used lm-eval-harness, zero-shot, batch size 1.

**BF16 (Qwen3 / released Orthrus / retrained Orthrus):**
- GSM8K: 0.4003 / 0.4238 / 0.4147
- HumanEval: 0.4024 / 0.3659 / 0.4146
- IFEval loose: 0.2015 / 0.2052 / 0.2181
- IFEval strict: 0.1682 / 0.1756 / 0.1830

**FP16:**
- GSM8K: 0.4261 / 0.4230 / 0.4170
- HumanEval: 0.4085 / 0.4085 / 0.4024
- IFEval loose: 0.2200 / 0.2052 / 0.2107
- IFEval strict: 0.1811 / 0.1682 / 0.1738

The authors say these gaps "should not be interpreted as statistically significant" and find no systematic degradation. In an example divergence, the only difference was "create" vs "cause."

- **Inference setup:** HF Transformers `generate()` (v5.8.1), PyTorch 2.8.0+cu128, CUDA 12.8, `attn_implementation="eager"`.
- **Hardware:** a single RTX 3090 (23 GB, compute capability 8.6).

## 2. Match rates and how they were measured
- **Prompts:** 1,190 across 12 domains (100 each; gec-en has 90).
- **Decoding:** greedy, `max_new_tokens=128`, `do_sample=False`.
- **Match definition:** a trajectory matches only if it has the same length and identical token indices as the reference.

| Precision | Released checkpoint | Retrained model |
|---|---|---|
| BF16 | 0.45 [0.42, 0.48] | 0.43 [0.40, 0.46] |
| FP16 | 0.87 [0.85, 0.89] | 0.87 [0.85, 0.89] |
| FP32 | 1.00 [0.997, 1.000] | 1.00 [0.997, 1.000] |

Brackets are 95% Wilson intervals.

- **BF16 by domain:** match rates range from 0.08 (poetry-en, retrained model) to 0.88 (gec-en).
- **Tokens per forward pass:** for example, math is 8.08 (released) vs 4.99 (retrained). The retrained model is higher in 10 of 12 domains.

## 3. Why divergence happens
The paper gives only a general explanation: "discrete token selection can amplify small numerical differences into divergent generation trajectories." The authors attribute it to finite precision "without attributing it to any particular layer or computational operation."

The paper does not analyze:
- differences between the verify and decode numerical paths,
- how tokens-per-forward relates to divergence,
- specific kernels.

**Correlate found:** divergence tracks the reference model's perplexity on the response.
- BF16 mean perplexity is 1.11 for matching vs 1.28 for diverging trajectories.
- In a logistic regression controlling for response length and domain, the log-perplexity coefficient is:
  - BF16: −8.10 (released) and −10.92 (retrained), with p ≤ 3×10⁻¹¹.
  - FP16: −3.93 and −3.78, with p < 0.01.

## 4. Cost of FP32
Not reported. The paper gives no speed or memory figures for FP32, and FP32 was used only for trajectory matching, not benchmarks.

## 5. Fixes other than FP32
None proposed. Localizing the responsible operation is listed as future work. Invariant kernels are not mentioned.

## 6. Related work on determinism
The only reproducibility citation is Yuan et al. (NeurIPS 2025), which shows that precision and system configuration "can alter outputs even under greedy decoding." No batch-invariance work is cited. Speculative-decoding citations include Leviathan et al. (2023), Draft&Verify, LayerSkip, Medusa, EAGLE, Gloeckle et al. (multi-token prediction), and DeepSeek-V3.

## 7. Downstream impact
Evaluation used lm-eval-harness, zero-shot, batch size 1.

**BF16 (Qwen3 / released Orthrus / retrained Orthrus):**
- GSM8K: 0.4003 / 0.4238 / 0.4147
- HumanEval: 0.4024 / 0.3659 / 0.4146
- IFEval loose: 0.2015 / 0.2052 / 0.2181
- IFEval strict: 0.1682 / 0.1756 / 0.1830

**FP16:**
- GSM8K: 0.4261 / 0.4230 / 0.4170
- HumanEval: 0.4085 / 0.4085 / 0.4024
- IFEval loose: 0.2200 / 0.2052 / 0.2107
- IFEval strict: 0.1811 / 0.1682 / 0.1738

The authors say these gaps "should not be interpreted as statistically significant" and find no systematic degradation. In an example divergence, the only difference was "create" vs "cause."

**Note:** The HTML rendering drops the system names. The proposed method and the baseline (Yuan et al. 2025, likely LayerCast) both appear as blanks.

**(1) Reduction order: K-only or M too?**
- The paper says the order is a function of shape: configs are "selected by a pure function of the problem shape (M,N,K)". There are two M-buckets: decode (M≤64) and prefill.
- **Within the decode bucket,** config and segmentation "depend only on K, never on the batch dimension M". This makes the kernel batch-invariant for M from 1 to 64.
  - Verified on all 18 (shape, GPU) cells.
  - Variants that size the split by occupancy or re-tune per M were invariant on only 4/18. cuBLAS was invariant on none.
- **Across the bucket boundary, it is not token-count invariant.** "row 0 changes at M=65 under every policy", including the proposed kernel, because M=65 switches to the prefill configuration.
- **Prefill:** only the decode bucket is claimed invariant. With R1 and R3 in force, BM, BN, warps and stages are "numerically inert". Only the split factor and BK change the bits.

**(2) Kernel design**
- **Fused upcast:** BF16 weight tiles are loaded from HBM and widened to FP32 in registers. No FP32 copy of the weights is materialized.
- **R1:** IEEE FMA only (`input_precision="ieee"`), with no tensor cores and no TF32.
- **R2:** No autotuning. Tile configs are compile-time constants, one for decode and one for prefill.
  - Decode example: (32,128,64).
  - Prefill tile: 128×128.
- **R3:** Deterministic split-K.
  - The split factor S depends only on K.
  - Partial sums are written to a workspace, then a second kernel sums them in ascending order with no atomics.
  - In the R2 tuning table, prefill uses S=1.

**(3) Performance**
- **vs. the baseline (end-to-end):** "1.17–1.43× on A100 and H100 and by 1.6–3.1× on L40S". The proposed kernel was faster in all 36 configurations.
- **Memory vs. the baseline:**
  - About 1–1.4 GiB less resident weight memory.
  - A smaller transient allocation spike: 0.051 vs 0.445 GiB on the 8B model.
  - 4–7% more KV-cache capacity.
- **vs. cuBLAS:**
  - In prefill, the Triton GEMM reaches "∼0.85× cuBLAS throughput".
  - IEEE FMA GEMMs are "2.4× slower than TF32 at the median decode shape and 5.6× slower" at the median prefill shape.
- **Decode-specific costs and gains:**
  - Ordered split-K is "1.9 to 5.6× faster than no split" and 4.2% faster than atomic split-K.
  - Pinning the config costs 1.4% at the median, with a worst case of 21.9% (lm_head on L40S).
  - Re-tuning per M would be 5–25% faster at M≤16 and 2–9% faster at M=32.
  - Just above the bucket boundary (M=65–128), a tuned kernel is "roughly 3× faster".
  - On the ragged probe shape, the pinned config is 29–70× slower than the best tuned one.
- **vs. vLLM / Thinking Machines batch-invariant kernels:** not benchmarked. The paper only cites their "∼20% matmul slowdown" and notes they remain architecture-dependent.

**(4) Hardware**
- NVIDIA only, single GPU: A100 PCIe 40GB, L40S PCIe, H100 PCIe.
- No AMD. Bitwise portability across vendors is called "an open problem".

**(5) Attention**
- Attention is not pinned. It uses vLLM 0.8's xFormers backend in FP32, which "may in principle select architecture-specific code paths".
- The one residual divergence (Qwen3-4B on GSM8K, 0.08%) traces to layer-0 attention on H100, which differs by "about 6×10⁻⁸".
- Logits matched bitwise on only 9.6% of positions when comparing against H100.

**(6) Speculative decoding**
- Not used. It appears only in the related-work citation of LLM-42, which uses "verified speculation" with rollback for same-architecture determinism.

## (1) GEMM reduction-order descriptor (GEMMDesc)

The descriptor is meant to record only what fixes the bits. The paper says it "holds nothing that is only a speed knob."

**Plain GEMM fields**
- `instruction_k`: how many products one MMA folds into a single rounding.
- `use_fast_accum`: whether the MMA result reaches the accumulator in one rounding or two.
- `k_loop_step`: whether the short remainder turn of the K loop runs first or last.

**Split-K fields**
- `k_cuts`: a nest of cuts, outermost first.
- `span`: the part length at each level of the nest.
- `partial_dtype` and `merge_dtype`: these are set independently. The options are fp32/fp32, output-type/fp32, or output/output.
- Worked example: in an fp16 GEMM on GB300 with K=576, the probe found three parts of 192.

**Other families**
- Chained chunks: two levels of span.
- GEMV: a strided vs. contiguous `layout`, plus a lane butterfly recorded per round.

**Which knobs change the bits**
- **BLOCK_M and BLOCK_N preserve bits.** Re-tiling only moves work between threads, and each output element keeps its own accumulator chain.
- **BLOCK_K also preserves bits on the tensor-core path, contrary to your premise.** The authors state "The three block sizes are speed knobs." It is `instruction_k` that matters, not BLOCK_K.
- **Exceptions where BLOCK_K-like chunking does matter:**
  - Re-chunking a scalar fold "regroups the sum."
  - In attention, BLOCK_N (and BLOCK_M under causal masking) is "a term of the arithmetic."
- **Split-K changes the bits** via span, cuts and merge dtypes.
- **MMA instruction choice:** on GB300, mma.sync and tcgen05.mma are bitwise equivalent at fp16 and bf16 but not at fp8. As a result, the descriptor names the instruction explicitly.
- **Other factors with no effect:** pipeline depth (`num_stages`) and warp specialization leave the dependence tree unchanged.

## (2) AMD experiments

- **No rocBLAS or hipBLASLt reconstruction.** The black-box work covers cuBLAS only, on GB300, GB200 and H100. rocBLAS appears only in background discussion; hipBLASLt is not mentioned.
- **What AMD work exists:**
  - An AMDGCN checker evaluated on gfx942 (CDNA3) over its own corpus of 4,500 configurations.
  - The Triton backend's wave64 pinned reduction, which uses `row_shr` steps in the order 1, 2, 4, 8 instead of 8, 4, 2, 1.
- MI200 and MI300 are never named.

## (3) Cost of fixed order and mitigation

The paper cites prior work estimating a cost of "about 20% of matrix-multiply throughput against cuBLAS."

**Reduction kernels (layout optimization)**
- 19 of 27 kernels land within 10% of free-order mode.
- On H100, six of ten reach or pass free-order, by up to 42% on an epilogue column sum.
- On GB300, it passes free-order once and otherwise reaches 57–99%.
- The text is inconsistent: the abstract says "5 even exceed," while elsewhere it says "five of the ten" and "six of ten."

**Standalone GEMM vs. cuBLAS**

| Size | Free-order (torch.compile) | Bit-exact | Accelerated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Above 5 GFLOP | 61–88% | 56–93% | 69–91% |
| Below 5 GFLOP | 59–88% | 50–100% | — |

**Fused epilogue (96 shapes)**
- torch.compile reaches 85–125% of the cuBLAS-plus-separate-epilogue baseline.
- The bit-exact fused kernel reaches 95–168%.
- The bit-exact kernel itself runs 1.8× longer than the baseline's kernel half; the win comes from removing one launch.

## (4) Static checker (PTX + AMD GCN)

- **Implementation:** about 2,500 lines of Python over a PTX parser, with an AMDGCN twin sharing the same tree representation.
- **Method:** a symbolic-thread walk with affine address evaluation, canonical sorting of commutative nodes, and a hash signature. It plugs into Triton's autotuner as a pruning predicate.
- **Soundness evidence:** 51,152 configurations on GB300 (47 kernels, five FP formats), with zero over-merges, plus 4,500 configurations on gfx942.
- **Over-split factor:**
  - 1.0 on GEMMs (exact partition).
  - 1.0–2.5 on reductions and norms.
  - 6.7–23.0 on four out-of-focus kernels.
  - 10.0 on flash attention.
- **Limitation:** soundness holds relative to the assembly (PTX or AMDGCN), not SASS.

## (5) Batch invariance, small M, decode, speculative decoding

- **Batch invariance** is defined in the introduction. The paper describes DeepSeek-V4 noting split-K is "taken only at small batch sizes and so batch-dependent."
- **Small M in the evaluation:**
  - The fuzzing set includes M=1.
  - The LM-head shapes use M from 1 to 256.
  - MoE shapes start at M=16.
- **Small M in the cuBLAS split-K tail bug:** examples include 1×8×8648, which loses 8 k-values, and 32×32 through 128×128 at K=11,528.
- **Decode and speculative decoding are not mentioned.**

======== NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM#19501 IS [2026-09-21] state=open comments=2 (rate rem 40)
TITLE: [RFC] Training/Inference Numerical Consistency for RL Post-Training
AUTHOR: shikicloud

## Motivation

In RL post-training, the rollout engine samples tokens and the trainer recomputes logprobs on those same tokens with the same weights. When the two disagree, PPO's importance ratio is computed against the wrong denominator; low-probability tokens can spike the ratio and blow up gradients; training can collapse.

Four causes, each with published evidence:

1. **Kernels are not batch-invariant.** The same request can produce different logits depending on what else is in the batch, because RMSNorm/matmul/attention pick their reduction strategy from batch shape ([Thinking Machines, "Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference"](https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/defeating-nondeterminism-in-llm-inference/), 2025-09-10).
2. **MoE routing disagrees between engines even with identical weights** — ~10% of per-layer routing decisions differ, 94% of tokens affected in ≥1 layer, on Qwen3-30B-A3B ([R3 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11370), arXiv 2510.11370). R3 (#18397) is an initial solution to fix this cause.
3. **LM-head / router precision.** BF16 alone dropped train/inference token-probability correlation to ~0.9; FP32 restored ~0.99 ([MiniMax-M1 tech report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13585), arXiv 2506.13585).
4. **Severity is hardware- and kernel-dependent and compounds with length.** Same code: KL ≈ 5e-4–1e-3 on one GPU, 1e-2–1e-1 on another, traced to a specific attention-kernel bug ([ByteDance Seed, "When Speed Kills Stability"](https://yingru.notion.site/When-Speed-Kills-Stability-Demystifying-RL-Collapse-from-the-Training-Inference-Mismatch-271211a558b7808d8b12d403fd15edda)).

R3 addresses cause 2. This RFC covers what's left of R3 (cause 2's remaining edges) plus causes 1, 3, and a sampling-semantics issue that compounds all of them. Other useful features like TIS/MIS/KPop remain in RL frameworks but not inference engines. Futhermore, this RFC targets on important features for TRTLLM, we will explore new features to solve this problem on an new issue.

This RFC is generated by codex with human's instructions and supervision. Also thanks @NolenLiang and @JeffPengCoder's help. CC's @joyang-nv @xuantengh @yuki-97 

## What exists today

**Most relevant: LLM-42 (arXiv, January 2026)**

I found several useful sources. Together they suggest that speculative decoding keeps the rollout on-policy in theory, but in practice the logprobs still need to match what the trainer computes.

**Why the mismatch matters**
- In RL post-training, the rollout engine samples tokens, and the trainer then recomputes logprobs for those same tokens with the same weights. When the two disagree, PPO's importance ratio is computed against the wrong denominator; low-probability tokens can spike the ratio and blow up gradients; training can collapse.
- One main cause is that kernels are not batch-invariant. The same request can produce different logits depending on what else is in the batch, because RMSNorm/matmul/attention pick their reduction strategy from batch shape.
- A September 2025 post on RL collapse names speculative decoding as one of the throughput tricks behind the problem: modern inference engines (e.g., vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM) employ aggressive optimization strategies like speculative decoding, low-precision computation (INT8/FP8), and specialized, batch-variant CUDA kernels.

**Speculative decoding in the RL loop**
- An arXiv paper (2604.26779) on adding speculative decoding to RL rollouts says log-probabilities, KL penalties, and the policy loss must be computed against the verifier (target) policy, not the draft; otherwise, speculative decoding would alter the optimization target. In their setup, the vLLM backend generates rollout trajectories using speculative decoding. The policy model (MegatronLM) then runs the forward pass used to compute the GRPO policy loss. They report it reduces this exposed generation time from 10.4 s to 0.6 s per step and lowers effective step time from 75.0 s to 60.5 s (1.24×).
- The EfficientRollout paper notes that SD speedups don't simply carry over to RL because the evolving target policy makes any fixed drafter increasingly mismatched with the policy's output distribution; and (ii) active batch sizes shrink throughout rollout decoding. Its drafter is a weight-quantized copy of the target model.
- TensorRT-LLM's RFC on train/inference numerical consistency says spec decode / MTP support fails closed today — draft/verification tokens need routing captured too, or the feature silently stops working the moment spec decode is turned on for rollout throughput.

**Bitwise parity and batch invariance**
- A Megatron-LM tracking issue aims for a zero train/generation log-prob gap: for the same weights and the same tokens, the training log-prob equals the generation log-prob bitwise, regardless of how many other tokens shared the launch (decode steps are a few tokens; the log-prob pass is a whole microbatch). This is the same shape problem that speculative verify passes run into, since they score several tokens per step. The issue also argues that importance-ratio clipping or truncation alone hides the mismatch rather than removing it, and it adds bias that is unrelated to the policy update.
- One open-source project reports the FP32 selected-token logprob bytes from trainer scoring, inference prefill and inference decode are bitwise-identical. It also says while SGLang has settings to trigger batch-invariant kernels, you can't get 0 train-infer mismatch with SGLang. The cost was real: on Qwen3-8B the bitwise-identical forward lowers sampling throughput by 16.2%. The gain was too: removing the mismatch improves the solve rate in our open-source RL stack from 63.9% to 77.4%.
- The Miles/SGLang team's write-up says the key to fully eliminating the mismatch is to align all the operator backends between training and rollout—making every operation in training and inference bitwise-identical. They also wrote a separate post on bringing speculative decoding into RL.

**Other relevant work**
- *LLM-42: Enabling Determinism in LLM Inference with Verified Speculation* (Gond et al.) and *Deterministic Inference across Tensor Parallel Sizes That Eliminates Training-Inference Mismatch* (Zhang et al.) are both cited on arxiv.org.
- ReSpec (arXiv 2510.26475) and FastGRPO also study speculative decoding for RL.
- A practical guide warns that sampling settings matter too: with top-p/top-k, vLLM samples from a truncated distribution while the Actor computes log‑probs over the full vocabulary.

**Bottom line:** The accept/reject step keeps the target distribution exact in theory, so speculative decoding doesn't make rollouts off-policy. The catch is that verify passes score several tokens at once, which changes the kernel shapes compared with the trainer's forward pass. Without batch-invariant kernels, the rollout logprobs won't match the trainer's bit for bit. Then you have to either recompute logprobs on the trainer side or apply importance-sampling corrections (TIS/MIS).
