I couldn't find any source saying that Miles' bitwise "true on-policy" mode has been confirmed to work together with MTP speculative decoding. The two features are documented separately, and the true-on-policy mode is officially limited to small Qwen3 dense models. Details below.

**What Miles is**
Miles is RadixArk's RL post-training framework, forked from and co-evolving with slime. The Miles v0.1 technical report (arXiv 2609.08368, Sept 2026) says it uses rollout engines built on SGLang and a trainer with a choice of two backends (NVIDIA Megatron-LM and PyTorch FSDP). Beyond full-parameter RL, it also supports LoRA RL, on-policy distillation, supervised fine-tuning, and true-on-policy rollout-training alignment.

**True on-policy and deterministic rollout**
- From the Nov 2025 launch blog: "Beyond deterministic inference (bitwise identical results), we now support true on-policy via an infrastructure approach. We've eliminated the mismatch between training and inference to exactuly 0 kl divergence." This uses Flash Attention 3, DeepGEMM, batch invariant kernels from Thinking Machines Lab, and torch.compile. They also aligned numeric operations between training and inference.
- Why it matters: even when the exact sampled tokens are preserved, different kernels and batch shapes can make rollout and trainer probabilities disagree. The true-on-policy alignment pins these computations so that, in supported configurations, the sampled-token log-probabilities are identical.
- Limits stated in the v0.1 report:
  - The exactness only applies to the supported Qwen3 dense 0.6B and 4B profiles, and only to sampled-token log-probabilities, not the whole output distribution or stale-weight data.
  - On Qwen3-4B-Base with DAPO prompts, the reward curve matches the baseline, but rollout takes longer.
  - The flagship GLM-5.2 run does not use exact alignment and leaves R3 off. It reports a mean train–rollout divergence of 0.0369 on sampled tokens over 100 steps and corrects for it with truncated importance sampling.
- There's also a Miles PR (#2920) titled "Make the rollout deterministic comparison prove what it claims".

**Speculative decoding and MTP in Miles**
- Freezing the draft model during RL keeps it from following the target model's policy, which lowers accept length and speedup. Miles instead runs online SFT on the draft model throughout RL, giving a 25%+ rollout speedup vs. a frozen MTP, especially late in training.
- On the training side it supports MTP with sequence packing + CP, loss masks with edge-case handling, LM head/embedding gradient isolation, and Megatron↔SGLang weight syncing.
- Items on the launch roadmap: compatibility with SGLang spec v2 and advanced speculative decoding (e.g., EAGLE3, multi-spec layer).
- For DeepSeek-V4, SGLang/Miles shipped MTP speculative decoding with in-graph metadata.

**Warnings from a third-party fork (Proximal Labs/miles)**
These are one team's findings, not official Miles results.
- Their reasoning on why the draft shouldn't affect RL correctness: serving uses the MTP head as the NEXTN draft, speculative sampling keeps the policy's output distribution exactly, and logprobs come from the full model's verification pass, so draft quality only affects decode speed.
- In practice they found problems. A sampling check found NEXTN speculative decoding with rejection sampling emits tokens the target gives logprob -24 to -34 in ~2% of speculated positions at 3 and 4 draft steps (random multilingual tokens mid-sentence); 0 in 7,200 without speculation. Returned logprobs are correct; the samples are not, which breaks rollout_logprobs behavior correction and the agent's output.
- Their fix was to switch to SGLang's default verification instead of rejection sampling, which showed no near-impossible tokens and sampled-token logprobs within noise.
- They also found a training-side bug: Miles only sets mtp_detach_heads under --enable-mtp-training. Without that flag the MTP layer reads the trunk's hidden states without detaching them, so the loss gradient reaches the policy's LoRA weights. The fix: make the Megatron-Bridge path build MTP layers only when --mtp-num-layers is set.

To confirm whether true-on-policy mode officially supports speculative decoding, the best places to check are the Miles docs at miles.radixark.com and Section 5.3 of the v0.1 report.

- There's also a Miles PR (#2920) titled "Make the rollout deterministic comparison prove what it claims".

**Speculative decoding and MTP in Miles**
- Freezing the draft model during RL keeps it from following the target model's policy, which lowers accept length and speedup. Miles instead runs online SFT on the draft model throughout RL, giving a 25%+ rollout speedup vs. a frozen MTP, especially late in training.
- On the training side it supports MTP with sequence packing + CP, loss masks with edge-case handling, LM head/embedding gradient isolation, and Megatron↔SGLang weight syncing.
- Items on the launch roadmap: compatibility with SGLang spec v2 and advanced speculative decoding (e.g., EAGLE3, multi-spec layer).
- For DeepSeek-V4, SGLang/Miles shipped MTP speculative decoding with in-graph metadata.

**Warnings from a third-party fork (Proximal Labs/miles)**
These are one team's findings, not official Miles results.
- Their reasoning on why the draft shouldn't affect RL correctness: serving uses the MTP head as the NEXTN draft, speculative sampling keeps the policy's output distribution exactly, and logprobs come from the full model's verification pass, so draft quality only affects decode speed.
- In practice they found problems. A sampling check found NEXTN speculative decoding with rejection sampling emits tokens the target gives logprob -24 to -34 in ~2% of speculated positions at 3 and 4 draft steps (random multilingual tokens mid-sentence); 0 in 7,200 without speculation. Returned logprobs are correct; the samples are not, which breaks rollout_logprobs behavior correction and the agent's output.
- Their fix was to switch to SGLang's default verification instead of rejection sampling, which showed no near-impossible tokens and sampled-token logprobs within noise.
- They also found a training-side bug: Miles only sets mtp_detach_heads under --enable-mtp-training. Without that flag the MTP layer reads the trunk's hidden states without detaching them, so the loss gradient reaches the policy's LoRA weights. The fix: make the Megatron-Bridge path build MTP layers only when --mtp-num-layers is set.

To confirm whether true-on-policy mode officially supports speculative decoding, the best places to check are the Miles docs at miles.radixark.com and Section 5.3 of the v0.1 report.

TITLE: [Tracking] Bitwise train/generation parity for RL: batch-invariant inference + the training forward
AUTHOR: YigongQin

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

In on-policy RL (GRPO and similar) the policy that samples rollouts (Megatron Inference) and the policy that scores them for the loss (the Megatron training forward) are the same weights run through different code. Any numerical gap between the two is a train/generation mismatch: it shows up as nonzero `gen_kl_error`, biases the importance ratio, and forces off-policy corrections that exist only because of kernel rounding rather than because the policy moved.

The target is a **zero train/generation log-prob gap**: for the same weights and the same tokens, the training log-prob equals the generation log-prob bitwise, regardless of how many other tokens shared the launch (decode steps are a few tokens; the log-prob pass is a whole microbatch).

**Describe the solution you'd like**

One tracking issue with the status of each piece below, kept up to date as PRs land. It does not propose new code on its own.

There are two properties, and both are needed:

1. **Batch invariance of generation.** A token's output does not depend on the batch it was launched in (`batch_invariant_mode`).
2. **Train/generation parity.** The training forward produces the same bits as generation for the same weights and the same token count.

### 1. Batch-invariant generation kernels

| PR / issue | What | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #4871 | Batch-invariant Nemotron (hybrid Mamba + MoE): batch-invariant MoE routing/permute, Mamba decode kernels, batch-invariant GEMM/norm kernels | merged |
| #6521 | Batch-invariant generation with the vLLM fused-MoE backend | merged |
| #7302 | MXFP8 batch invariance for inference and TE grouped training | merged |
| #7300 | Selective MXFP8 inference precision | merged |
| #6859 | Fix the batch-invariant RMSNorm forward and its input gradient | open |
| #6933 | TE MXFP8 grouped MoE inference backend | open |
| #7830 | `flashinfer_mega` generation backend (FlashInfer `moe_ep` megakernel, BF16/MXFP8/NVFP4/FP8_FP4); composes with `batch_invariant_mode`. Also listed under 2. | open |
| #7650 / #7651 | Batch-invariant weighted SwiGLU reads invalid memory at large input offsets (bug / fix) | open |
| #7659 / #7660 | Fuse batch-invariant MoE permutation with MXFP8 quantization (perf, must stay bit-exact) | open |

### 2. Making the training forward match generation

| PR | What | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #7562 | Bitwise train/generation parity for batch-invariant hybrid (Mamba + MoE) models: squared-ReLU rounding, Mamba kernel and gate placement | open, approved |
| #7798 | `moe_inference_training_forward`: the MoE training value pass runs the inference expert kernel (`vllm`, `torch` backends, BF16 and MXFP8) and the backward comes from the TE recompute pass | open |
| #7830 | `flashinfer_mega` backend for that mode (also a batch-invariant generation kernel, see 1): FlashInfer `moe_ep` megakernel (fused EP transport + SwiGLU expert MLP), BF16 and MXFP8; stacked on #7798 | open |

The idea in #7798/#7830 is to stop hand-reproducing each inference kernel's rounding in the training path and instead run the inference kernel itself for the value, while the gradient stays TE's (straight-through under MXFP8).

### 3. Adjacent RL numerics (not parity-specific, but they show up in the same metric)

| PR | What | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #7182 | Sample via Gumbel-max exponential race in fp32 | merged |
| #6723 | Refresh the Mamba decode cache after a refit | open |

### What has been validated

<FILL IN: keep this section to results that are linked and reproducible.>

* Unit tests: bitwise train/generation parity per precision (BF16, MXFP8), in train and eval mode, across token counts under batch-invariant mode; kernel determinism replays registered in `tests/unit_tests/determinism/kernels/`.
* End to end in NeMo-RL: `gen_kl_error` of 0.0000 on <FILL IN: model(s), steps, W&B links> for the generic mode (#7798), and <FILL IN: model, steps, W&B link> for the mega backend (#7830), where BF16 and MXFP8 mega runs match the original BF16 path. <FILL IN: figures.>

### Known gaps and open questions

* **MXFP8 refit asymmetry.** Generation's MXFP8 weights are quantized on the receiver from BF16 slices, while the training value pass quantizes the whole local parameter. MXFP8 scales are per 32-element block, so the two need not land on the same bits. The unit tests start both sides from the same weights and do not cover this. <FILL IN: result of an end-to-end refit check, if any.>
* **Straight-through gradient.** Under MXFP8 the training value is quantized while the gradient is the BF16 function's. This is by design and opt-in; it is not a parity gap, but it is a semantic difference from a native MXFP8 backward.
* **Training-side backends.** The mode covers `vllm`, `torch` and `flashinfer_mega`. The non-mega `flashinfer` backend is rejected (it reads a shuffled copy derived from the parameters with no per-forward rebuild). `nvfp4` and `fp8_fp4` g

content.content:
**Date and authors**
- The post is dated August 17, 2026, per its bibtex entry. The sole author is Ashwinee Panda.
- Qingyang Wu and Zhongzhu Zhou are thanked as XoRL contributors, and TogetherAI supplied the compute.

**What is made bitwise identical**
- The guarantee is stronger than K3=0: "the FP32 selected-token logprob bytes from trainer scoring, inference prefill and inference decode are bitwise-identical."
- The engines are XoRL (trainer) and a fork of SGLang (inference).
- For cached state: "Training, prefill, eager decode and CUDA-graph decode all write state, and all four have to write the same bytes."
- Sampling transforms (temperature, top-k, top-p, min-p) are replayed in the trainer as a full program, not as a mask.

**How it's done**
There are four methods:
1. Call the SGLang forward kernel inside XoRL and write a custom backward.
2. Add one shared kernel to both engines.
3. Make reductions batch-invariant.
4. Write two kernels that do identical arithmetic.

Key kernels:
- **RoPE:** A full FP32 table is built on the CPU, because CPU and GPU tables diverged at position 593. The rotation stays in FP32 with one BF16 round ("Class B").
- **RMSNorm:** A new shared kernel uses an explicit tree reduction instead of `tl.sum`, because a residual store changed Triton's `sizePerThread` from [4] to [8]. That one change altered "2,854 of 8,192 outputs."
- **GEMM:** A Triton kernel accumulates the full K dimension left to right in 64-value slabs with one FP32 accumulator and no split-K. Larger M just "launches more of the same work." DeepGEMM is used where it produces the same bits and runs faster.
- **SwiGLU:** A one-round kernel computes in FP32 and casts to BF16 once.
- **Attention:** FlashAttention 4 with `num_splits=1` in both engines.
- **LM head:** 256-logit groups and a fixed merge tree.
- **Pinned vs. free parameters:** Only parameters that set reduction shape are pinned. Row-block size, stages and warps remain free per engine.

Small-M and decode-specific handling:
- **RMSNorm:** With only a few very wide rows, the same calculation is split across three launches.
- **Gated DeltaNet decode:** Decode restarts from the stored 64-row chunk boundary and recomputes "at most 64 rows," with cached rows reused inside CUDA graphs.
- **MXFP4 Marlin experts:** Both engines run the packed GEMMs "one row at a time," because Marlin's bits vary with row count.
- **DeepSeek-V4 sparse prefill:** The prefill kernel is not byte-stable, so the prompt is replayed by looping the decode kernel once per row.

Parallelism:
- Expert-parallel outputs are exchanged without reduction, then summed with an explicit pairwise tree in FP64 using logical (data-parallel-major) ordering. DeepEP is used only for communication.
- Context parallelism uses Ulysses for dense attention. GDN is split only on 64-token chunk boundaries.
- Pipeline boundaries pass BF16 rows that already include the residual.

**Measured overhead (sampling throughput)**

| Model | Flags off | Bitwise-identical | Ablations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-8B | 2,116 tok/s | 1,774 tok/s (0.839×) | 1,970 without batch-invariant dense GEMMs |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 7,863 tok/s | 4,767 tok/s (−39.4%, +57.9% wall time) | 5,778 aligned except GDN |
| GLM-5.2 (TP16/EP16/CP16) | 147.6 tok/s | 107.2 tok/s (−27.4%) | 125.9 without expert path; 110.2 without sparse selector; 105.8 without batch-invariant dense GEMMs |
| DeepSeek-V4 (TP8/DP8/EP8, one node) | 46.0 tok/s | 40.2 tok/s (−12.7%) | 42.5 without expert path |

- **End-to-end step time** (Qwen3.6, flags-off CISPO vs. zero-K3): 374.3 s vs. 447.0 s, about 20%. Excluding weight sync, 334.8 s vs. 409.9 s.

**RL benefit (Wordle, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B)**
- **Zero mismatch vs. XoRL importance-sampling baseline:** held-out solve rate rises from 63.9% to 77.4%. Training solve at step 128 rises from 58.1% to 70.8%.
- **Other held-out results:**
  - River baseline: 76.4%
  - Tinker IS: 49.2%
  - XoRL CISPO: 72.5%
  - Tinker CISPO: 75.5%
  - PPO: 20.2%
  - Total Router Recall: 77.2%
  - River replaying expert IDs only: 74.8%
- **Async runs:** async + CISPO reached 59.4% held-out; adding Total Router Recall brought it to 76.6%.
- **Tinker instability:** 2 of 3 Tinker runs diverged at step 62. In one, a single token with a ratio of 19,276.5 carried 65.7% of squared coefficient mass.
- **Streaming RL:** saves 46% of serial wall time. Combining PipelineRL with Streaming RL gave a 244.0 s warm cycle vs. 338.5 s (1.39×).

**Hardware**
- No GPU model is stated. The only clue is that the Triton analysis compiled "against a fixed sm90 target" (Hopper).
- Parallel layouts are given as above: TP16/EP16/CP16 for GLM and one TP8/DP8/EP8 node for DeepSeek-V4.

**Speculative decoding, MTP and verify passes**
- None of these are mentioned in the provided content. The page is truncated at the appendix, so coverage there can't be confirmed.

=== 2510.26788v1 [2025-10-30] Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16
Comment: 
Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) often suffers from instability due to the numerical mismatch between the training and inference policies. While prior work has attempted to mitigate this issue through algorithmic corrections or engineering alignments, we show that its root cause lies in the floating point precision itself. The widely adopted BF16, despite its large dynamic range, introduces large rounding errors that breaks the consistency between training and inference. In this work, we demonstrate that simply reverting to \textbf{FP16} effectively eliminates this mismatch. The change is simple, fully supported by modern frameworks with only a few lines of code change, and requires no modification to the model architecture or learning algorithm. Our results suggest that using FP16 uniformly yields more stable optimization, faster convergence, and stronger performance across diverse tasks, algorithms and frameworks. We hope these findings motivate a broader reconsideration of precision trade-offs in RL fine-tuning.

=== 2609.32444v1 [2026-09-26] Rethinking Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning: Where It Arises and How to Correct It
Comment: 32 pages. Code: https://github.com/kzhao5/CIS-RL
We study training-inference mismatch in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for large language models, where rollouts are sampled by an inference engine while gradients are computed by a training engine, and the two engines assign different probabilities to the same tokens. To account for this discrepancy in policy updates, we introduce calibrated importance sampling (CIS). CIS is motivated by an empirically supported logit-displacement characterization that expresses the mismatch as an additive displacement $\varepsilon_t$ in log-odds, determined by the per-logit perturbation before the softmax, whose distribution is approximately invariant to token confidence. This characterization motivates a confidence-aware truncation: large positive displacements are truncated at a single constant threshold, which maps back to an importance-ratio cap that tightens as token confidence increases. Theoretically, we show that CIS replaces the unbounded second moment that governs the error of exact importance sampling with a term bounded by a constant, at the cost of a bias controlled by the truncated excess. In evaluation across three mixture-of-experts models and five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CIS achieves the highest five-benchmark average on all three models among the evaluated baselines. Diagnostic analyses show that CIS places less truncation bias on low-confidence tokens than truncated importance sampling, while upward clipping of small importance weights reduces held-out accuracy.

=== 2604.22411v1 [2026-04-24] Introducing Background Temperature to Characterise Hidden Randomness in Large Language Models
Comment: 
Even when decoding with temperature $T=0$, large language models (LLMs) can produce divergent outputs for identical inputs. Recent work by Thinking Machines Lab highlights implementation-level sources of nondeterminism, including batch-size variation, kernel non-invariance, and floating-point non-associativity. In this short note we formalize this behavior by introducing the notion of \emph{background temperature} $T_{\mathrm{bg}}$, the effective temperature induced by an implementation-dependent perturbation process observed even when nominal $T=0$. We provide clean definitions, show how $T_{\mathrm{bg}}$ relates to a stochastic perturbation governed by the inference environment $I$, and propose an empirical protocol to estimate $T_{bg}$ via the equivalent temperature $T_n(I)$ of an ideal reference system. We conclude with a set of pilot experiments run on a representative pool from the major LLM providers that demonstrate the idea and outline implications for reproducibility, evaluation, and deployment.

=== 2609.08368v1 [2026-09-08] Miles v0.1: Production-Level Post-Training
Comment: 34 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Technical report
We present Miles v0.1, a full-stack, production-ready system for frontier post-training. Building upon the clean design of slime, Miles designs each stage of the reinforcement-learning (RL) training loop around a single principle: components should be verified, clean, and customizable. With accuracy, efficiency, reliability, and scalability as first-class goals, Miles aims to make frontier-scale RL accessible to researchers and enterprises alike. This report walks through the system end to end: rollout engines built on SGLang, a trainer with a choice of two backends (NVIDIA Megatron-LM and PyTorch FSDP), and three weight-synchronization transports for different deployment topologies. Beyond full-parameter RL, Miles also supports LoRA RL, on-policy distillation, supervised fine-tuning, and true-on-policy rollout-training alignment, and extends the same architecture to diffusion models. We close with an end-to-end case study: fully asynchronous agentic RL on a GLM-5.2 744B-A40B model over terminal-use coding tasks, running on 64 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs with a median step time of 263 seconds over the first 30 measured steps. Miles is open-sourced at https://github.com/radixark/miles, with the project website at https://miles.radixark.com.

=== 2609.35140v1 [2026-09-28] AReaL-TIK: Stateful Agentic Optimization of Unified RL Kernels through an Optimization IR
Comment: 
Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training often uses distinct GPU kernels for rollout and policy update. In synchronous PPO and GRPO, numerical disagreement can perturb ratios between current token probabilities and those assigned during rollout. Recomputing rollout log-probabilities with the policy-update backend avoids this discrepancy but adds a forward pass. Bitwise-consistent unified kernels permit reuse when the policy snapshot and probability processing match the objective. Their optimization must preserve agreement across distinct execution regimes. We present KernelBraid, an agentic framework starting from a hand-tuned, bitwise-consistent implementation. Its optimization intermediate representation (IR) organizes source-code search by linking implementations and modifications to numerical requirements, workload measurements, and derivation history. The agent coordinates changes and retains verified intermediates for further exploration; promotion requires passing correctness checks and improving aggregate latency within per-workload limits. Across 12 end-to-end training configurations on H20, KernelBraid achieves 1.10x average throughput relative to AReaL with log-probability recomputation, and the mean training-reward ratio rounds to 1.00x. Isolated-layer profiling yields 1.40x average speedup in summed phase time across 15 model-GPU pairs. Operator-level evaluation covers correctness and performance for 10 operators on A100, H20, and H200, all passing the prescribed bitwise checks. Unified-attention search achieves 2.52x speedup in summed workload latency over the starting implementation using 7M LLM tokens; ablations assess the contributions of retained evidence and branch exploration to search efficiency and attained performance. Our code is open-sourced at

I couldn't find a page that uses the exact phrase "not identical" together with numerical differences in batched forward passes. What I did find is the documented verification mechanism, plus GitHub issues where users report that assisted decoding doesn't match plain greedy decoding.

**How assisted generation checks candidate tokens**
- A small assistant model drafts candidate tokens, and the main model checks these tokens in one pass. Validated tokens enter the final output and rejected tokens trigger standard sampling.
- From the original HF blog post: the main model uses .argmax() for greedy search or .multinomial() for sampling to get the next_tokens from logits, then compares next_tokens to candidates and counts the matching tokens. After the first mismatch, all candidates are invalidated.
- The docs say speculative decoding supports greedy search and sampling but not batched inputs.

**Reports of output that differs from greedy**
- **Issue #30413, "Assisted decoding results are not correct" (April 2024, transformers 4.40.0.dev0):** The user expected the same output as greedy and found that the candidate generator has the same output as greedy search but the target model (self) forward results are incorrect. They also noted that the cache_position is inconsistent. Their test used Llama-2-7b-chat as its own assistant with `num_assistant_tokens=1`.
- **Issue #30448, prompt lookup decoding vs. standard decoding (April 2024, transformers 4.40.1):** With greedy decoding in float32, PLD gave different outputs from standard decoding. The same happened with Llama 2, but not with an older transformers version under the same settings. That points to a regression rather than just floating-point noise.

**Why small differences can still happen (my explanation, not from the sources above)**
Even when the code is correct, scoring several candidate tokens in one forward pass uses different tensor shapes than generating one token at a time. That can change which GPU kernels run and the order in which floating-point numbers are added, so the logits come out very slightly different. This matters most in fp16/bf16. When the top two tokens have almost the same logit, a tiny difference can flip the argmax, and the two outputs then go different ways. So assisted generation should match greedy decoding in theory, but you can't expect bit-for-bit identical output. A genuine bug, like the cache-position problem in #30413, usually shows up as much bigger differences, even in float32.

If you meant a specific doc or code comment with that wording, it may be in the `generation/utils.py` source or the assisted-decoding tests, and I can look for it.

I couldn't find the exact README note you described. The search results show the Spec-Bench README's output-equality check, but not its wording about floating-point precision. That point is made clearly in the Spec-Bench paper and in other sources, though.

**Spec-Bench README (GitHub, hemingkx/Spec-Bench)**
- The README includes a step to examine whether the generated results are equal to autoregressive decoding or not, using a command like `python evaluation/equal.py --file-path /your_own_path/model_answer/ --jsonfile1 vicuna.jsonl --jsonfile2 eagle.jsonl`.
- The codebase is built from Medusa and EAGLE. Recent updates include: "2025.04.22: We have updated Leaderboard in Spec-Bench. 2025.03.23: We have integrated EAGLE-3 into Spec-Bench."

**The precision point (Spec-Bench paper, "Unlocking Efficiency in LLM Inference," ACL 2024 Findings)**
- In FP32 precision, the outputs of Speculative Decoding are guaranteed to be exactly the same as autoregressive decoding.
- But most Speculative Decoding approaches are predominantly evaluated using FP16 precision, and the authors stress that the outputs generated by Speculative Decoding in FP16 precision may not consistently align with those derived from autoregressive decoding.
- The paper includes a figure comparing the speedup of various methods on Spec-Bench with different computational precision. Its main results were obtained using Vicuna-7B-v1.3 at FP16 precision on a single NVIDIA 3090 GPU with a batch size of 1.
- In those results, EAGLE achieves the largest speedup (1.8x–2.4x) over autoregressive decoding across most subtasks, especially mathematical reasoning (about 2.4x).

**Other sources saying the same thing**
- vLLM docs: "While vLLM strives to ensure losslessness in speculative decoding, variations in generated outputs with and without speculative decoding can occur". The reasons given are floating-point precision and batch-size effects: changes in batch size may cause variations in logprobs and output probabilities, possibly from non-deterministic batched operations or numerical instability.
- A 2025–26 paper on batch speculative decoding, tested on SpecBench: its method reaches 3x throughput at batch size 8 with 95% exact match to standard decoding, and the remaining differences come from floating-point non-determinism, not synchronization errors. It also found that SGLang-EAGLE-Deterministic raised the match rate on Vicuna from 69.8% to 85.0%, which suggests most differences come from floating-point non-determinism rather than algorithm bugs.

**Bottom line:** EAGLE and other speculative decoding methods are lossless in theory. In FP16/BF16, though, small rounding differences can flip greedy argmax choices, so a token-by-token comparison (like Spec-Bench's `equal.py`) can show mismatches against plain autoregressive decoding. Running in FP32 should make the outputs identical, according to the Spec-Bench authors.

# Findings from "Batch Speculative Decoding Done Right" (arXiv 2510.22876v3)

## (1) Exact-match (E) and partial-match (P) rates

**Table 1** is measured against a batch=1 non-speculative baseline. It reports batch sizes 1 and 4 only. Values are E / P.

| Method | Vicuna BS1 | Vicuna BS4 | Qwen3 BS1 | Qwen3 BS4 | GLM4 BS1 | GLM4 BS4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Non-Spec-Batch | – | 53.8 / 98.2 | – | 92.9 / 96.5 | – | 93.3 / 97.2 |
| Spec-1 (HF) | 97.1 / 98.4 | – | 94.6 / 97.2 | – | 96.0 / 98.0 | – |
| EqSpec | 97.3 / 98.6 | 92.1 / 98.6 | 94.6 / 96.9 | 92.3 / 95.7 | 96.7 / 98.1 | 96.5 / 98.3 |
| EXSpec | 97.3 / 98.6 | 90.8 / 97.6 | 94.6 / 96.9 | 95.0 / 97.1 | 96.7 / 98.1 | 95.2 / 97.7 |
| DSD | 0.0 / 8.1 | 0.0 / 2.2 | 0.2 / 2.2 | 0.0 / 0.6 | 0.0 / 1.0 | 0.0 / 0.8 |
| BSP | 1.9 / 39.7 | 0.2 / 31.3 | 3.5 / 19.9 | 2.1 / 12.6 | 1.0 / 15.3 | 0.6 / 8.1 |

A notable detail: plain non-speculative batching at BS4 on Vicuna reaches only 53.8% exact match. This suggests batching alone causes divergence.

**Table 5** covers the continuous-batching systems. Each is compared against its own non-speculative mode, and no per-batch-size split is given.

| System | Vicuna | Qwen3 | GLM4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| vLLM + Spec | 96.9 / 98.0 | 65.6 / 78.5 | 72.7 / 84.5 |
| SGLang + EAGLE | 69.8 / 79.5 | 47.7 / 65.4 | – |
| SGLang + EAGLE + Det | 85.0 / 90.0 | 50.6 / 69.5 | – |

EAGLE was tested only through SGLang. The drafters were EAGLE2 for Vicuna and EAGLE3 for Qwen3, and GLM-4 had no available weights. The authors stress these systems solve "a fundamentally different problem than the static batch speculative decoding addressed in this paper."

## (2) SGLang-EAGLE-Deterministic

- **Flag:** The paper never names the flag. It only says it tested SGLang "with deterministic mode enabled" and cites the SGLang Team's Sept 2025 blog.
- **Build:** The authors compiled SGLang commit c4e314f from source because the feature "had not merged to the stable version."
- **Effect:** Vicuna exact match rose from 69.8% to 85.0% (partial 79.5 → 90.0). Qwen3 improved only from 47.7% to 50.6%.
- **Authors' reading:** The Vicuna gain "confirms that most divergences stem from floating-point non-determinism … rather than algorithmic bugs."

## (3) Explanation of residual divergence

The authors attribute the remaining ≈5% to "numerical non-determinism in floating-point operations" and to "tie-breaking in argmax sampling rather than algorithmic errors." They cite He & Thinking Machines Lab (2025) and Gond et al. (2026). They add support from Liu et al. (2025b), who found output length varies across batch sizes "due to kernel-level nondeterminism even in functionally correct implementations."

**Not in the text:** The paper does not explicitly explain the divergence in terms of differing tensor shapes between verify and decode passes. That mechanism is not described in this content.

## (4) Hardware and precision

- **Hardware/software:** NVIDIA A100 80GB, PyTorch 2.7, HF Transformers 4.51.3.
- **Precision and decoding:** All models were loaded in FP16 with greedy decoding (temperature=0, top_p=1.0) and five draft tokens per round.
- **Models:**
  - lmsys/vicuna-7b-v1.3 with double7/vicuna-68m
  - Qwen/Qwen3-8B with Qwen3-0.6B
  - zai-org/GLM-4-9B-0414 with jukofyork/GLM-4.5-DRAFT-0.6B-v3.0
- **Production systems:** vLLM 0.9.1 on the V0 engine, since V1 lacks draft-model speculative decoding.

## Purpose

Add per-architecture-family tuned bf16 launch configurations for the
batch-invariant `matmul_kernel_persistent` path on Hopper and Ada. The table
covers the five Qwen3-1.7B weight shapes, selects `BLOCK_SIZE_M`,

tile, making the invariance-critical constraint—fixed K-reduction order across

capability: SM 9.x selects `hopper`, SM 8.9 selects `ada`, and every other
capability keeps the existing default configuration unchanged.

# [Bugfix] Select batch-invariant matmul configs from runtime M under `torch.compile`

Fixes #54243.

## Problem

The tuned batch-invariant matmul table is keyed by `(architecture, N, K, M bucket)`,
but Dynamo evaluates the Python lookup while tracing. The resulting Triton tile is
therefore fixed in a dynamic graph even though `M` remains a runtime value.

## What this changes

- Route only compiled BF16 shapes that have tuned table entries through a vLLM
  custom op. Its implementation runs after tracing and selects the tile from the
  actual runtime `M`.
- Keep eager execution, FP16/FP32, architectures without a table, and untuned
  `(N, K)` shapes on the existing path.
- Prewarm the reachable table specializations before inference so runtime dispatch
  does not introduce Triton JIT compilation after vLLM enables its JIT monitor.
- Add tests for runtime `M=8`/`M=2048` selection in one compiled graph, bias,
  fallback paths, custom-op schema, real Triton correctness/bitwise invariance, and
  warmup coverage.

This does not change table contents, tuning policy, eager behavior, or public APIs.

## Validation

- `python -m pytest -q tests/v1/determinism/test_matmul_batch_invariant.py`
    - `34 passed, 8 skipped`
- All applicable pre-commit hooks passed for the three changed files.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B completed compiled V1 inference on SM120 with BF16, default
  `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` CUDA Graph mode, compile range `(1, 8192)`, and
  `jit_monitor_mode="error"`.
- A second process using the same cache reported direct binary graph-cache loading
  and completed strict-JIT inference. The unpatched upstream control loaded its
  graph cache but failed on the first request with inference-time JIT of
  `matmul_kernel_persistent`.

The SM120 check deliberately selected the existing upstream Ada table because SM120
does not yet have an upstream table. It validates control flow and JIT coverage, not
Ada performance.

table-wide cold-start cost before marking this ready. The local check does not cover

TITLE: [Perf] Use breakable CUDA graphs (no torch.compile) by default under VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT so the tuned matmul configs see the runtime M

## Purpose

`VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` routes every linear layer through the batch-invariant persistent Triton matmul, which picks its tile config from a per-architecture table keyed by `(N, K)` and an **M bucket** (#53247 Ada/Hopper, #53649 SM100, #57456 SM120). On the default `torch.compile` path that lookup (`_get_matmul_config`, called from `matmul_persistent`) runs while Dynamo traces the model with the compile-time dummy M, and the selected `BLOCK_M / BLOCK_N / num_warps / num_stages` are frozen in the graph. Every decode step therefore runs with the largest bucket's configs (#54243): on RTX PRO 6000 that is 3-6x slower per GEMM than the `M <= 8` configs the tables were tuned for, and it is where essentially all of the remaining batch-invariance overhead goes ([profile](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/54243#issuecomment-5723774275)).

Without `torch.compile` the lookup executes at CUDA graph capture time with each capture size's real M, and the tables work as intended. This PR makes batch-invariant mode default to that path via the existing breakable CUDA graph mechanism (#42304, `VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH=1`), following the same opt-in pattern as `default_breakable_cudagraph_architectures`. I couldn't find a ROCm Blogs post about deterministic or batch-invariant inference on MI300X. Neither the ROCm blog index nor its LLM tag page showed one. The work does exist in other places, though:

**vLLM: batch invariance on ROCm (PR #52231, by an AMD developer)**
- This PR enables broad-based batch invariant inference on ROCm, keyed by VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1.
- All-reduce and reduce-scatter (the steps that combine results across GPUs) are supported via CustomAllReduce and CustomReduceScatter. The 1stage algorithm is already batch-invariant, and the 2stage algorithm can be made batch-invariant by a one-line change. A corresponding fallback via all-gather and fixed-order sum is added that supports all platforms.
- On ROCm gfx950, custom all-reduce / reduce-scatter have been measured to be on par with if not faster than the RCCL implementations. Triton kernels have been added for batch-invariant softmax / scaled FP8 GEMM. Note that gfx950 is the MI350X/MI355X chip, not the MI300X.
- A reviewer pointed out a limit: the current AMD CI runs with TP=1, so these paths are not directly exercised. In other words, the multi-GPU paths aren't tested automatically yet.

**SGLang: deterministic inference (issue #10278)**
- The tracking issue includes deterministic all-reduce kernels (AMD) [amd] Add deterministic all-reduce kernel for AMD (ROCm) #15340.
- The Triton attention backend uses fixed decoding split sizes with manual alignment, enabling AMD hardware support. Users can enable deterministic inference with --enable-deterministic-inference --attention-backend [fa3|flashinfer|triton]. FA3 and FlashInfer are CUDA-focused, so on AMD the Triton backend is the one to use.

**Background**
- This all builds on Thinking Machines Lab's research. They found that output changes with server load because our forward pass lacks "batch invariance", causing our request's output to depend on the batch size of our forward pass. Thus, we only need to worry about the 3 operations that involve reductions — RMSNorm, matrix multiplication, and attention.
- Newer research: arXiv:2605.30218, first submitted on May 28, 2026, is titled MarginGate: Sparse Margin-Triggered Verification for Batch-Invariant LLM Inference. It generates tokens using a fast, non-deterministic path, and then ensures determinism through lightweight verification and rollback processes.

**Related ROCm/vLLM posts from 2026 (not about determinism)**
- vLLM's February 2026 blog on ROCm attention backends says vLLM now provides 7 attention backends on AMD ROCmTM software. It mentions that in the ROCM_AITER_FA design, execution paths are deterministic, making performance analysis straightforward. That's about predictable performance, not identical outputs regardless of batch size.

To get batch-invariant inference on MI300X today, the practical options are `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` in a vLLM build that includes PR #52231, or SGLang with `--enable-deterministic-inference --attention-backend triton`.

results:
I couldn't find a ROCm Blogs post about deterministic or batch-invariant inference on MI300X. Neither the ROCm blog index nor its LLM tag page showed one. The work does exist in other places, though:

**vLLM: batch invariance on ROCm (PR #52231, by an AMD developer)**
- This PR enables broad-based batch invariant inference on ROCm, keyed by VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1.
- All-reduce and reduce-scatter (the steps that combine results across GPUs) are supported via CustomAllReduce and CustomReduceScatter. The 1stage algorithm is already batch-invariant, and the 2stage algorithm can be made batch-invariant by a one-line change. A corresponding fallback via all-gather and fixed-order sum is added that supports all platforms.
- On ROCm gfx950, custom all-reduce / reduce-scatter have been measured to be on par with if not faster than the RCCL implementations. Triton kernels have been added for batch-invariant softmax / scaled FP8 GEMM. Note that gfx950 is the MI350X/MI355X chip, not the MI300X.
- A reviewer pointed out a limit: the current AMD CI runs with TP=1, so these paths are not directly exercised. In other words, the multi-GPU paths aren't tested automatically yet.

**SGLang: deterministic inference (issue #10278)**
- The tracking issue includes deterministic all-reduce kernels (AMD) [amd] Add deterministic all-reduce kernel for AMD (ROCm) #15340.
- The Triton attention backend uses fixed decoding split sizes with manual alignment, enabling AMD hardware support. Users can enable deterministic inference with --enable-deterministic-inference --attention-backend [fa3|flashinfer|triton]. FA3 and FlashInfer are CUDA-focused, so on AMD the Triton backend is the one to use.

**Background**
- This all builds on Thinking Machines Lab's research. They found that output changes with server load because our forward pass lacks "batch invariance", causing our request's output to depend on the batch size of our forward pass. Thus, we only need to worry about the 3 operations that involve reductions — RMSNorm, matrix multiplication, and attention.
- Newer research: arXiv:2605.30218, first submitted on May 28, 2026, is titled MarginGate: Sparse Margin-Triggered Verification for Batch-Invariant LLM Inference. It generates tokens using a fast, non-deterministic path, and then ensures determinism through lightweight verification and rollback processes.

**Related ROCm/vLLM posts from 2026 (not about determinism)**
- vLLM's February 2026 blog on ROCm attention backends says vLLM now provides 7 attention backends on AMD ROCmTM software. It mentions that in the ROCM_AITER_FA design, execution paths are deterministic, making performance analysis straightforward. That's about predictable performance, not identical outputs regardless of batch size.

To get batch-invariant inference on MI300X today, the practical options are `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` in a vLLM build that includes PR #52231, or SGLang with `--enable-deterministic-inference --attention-backend triton`.

{"notes":[{"content":{"venue":{"value":"ICLR 2027 Conference Submission"},"keywords":{"value":["speculative decoding","large language model inference","numerical precision","deterministic inference","execution-level equivalence"]},"primary_area":{"value":"foundation or frontier models, including LLMs"},"abstract":{"value":"Speculative decoding is lossless at the level of the decoding rule, but this guarantee does not require different finite-precision executions to produce identical decisions. We study this distinction in greedy speculative decoding and focus on an attribution problem: when speculative and autoregressive generation disagree, does the disagreement arise specifically under speculative verification, or is the same state already sensitive to the autoregressive execution path? We address this question with a three-way diagnostic that compares incremental autoregressive execution ($A$), full-prefix autoregressive execution ($B$), and speculative verification ($C$) at the same token prefix. We treat $A=B\neq C$ as verifier-specific disagreement relative to these two matched autoregressive controls. Among 555 reconstructed first-divergence events in Qwen3, 166 satisfy this criterion, while 389 are already autoregressive-path-sensitive. Across Qwen3, SmolLM2, and Pythia, all 1,850 reconstructed BF16 divergence events collapse to $A=B=C$ under backend-matched FP32 replay, which we use only as a diagnostic control. The observed bifurcations are strongly enriched near low-margin decisions, but their prevalence also varies with execution shape and backend. The results therefore do not support a universal margin threshold or block-size law. A targeted replication on A100/Ampere again identifies the same event class at both tested block sizes, and all 145 reconstructed events collapse under matched FP32 replay. The verifier-specific fraction is nevertheless lower than on RTX4090/Ada, showing that the event class persists across the two tested GPU architectures while its observed magnitude can differ. We further use Selective Canonical Re-verification as a mechanism-grounded intervention. Changing only the execution realization recovers most lost execution identity in most tested settings, while high-margin residuals expose the limits of margin-only selection and direct GPU timing quantifies the cost of the present implementation. These results separate two notions of exactness: losslessness constrains the decoder, whereas execution identity also depends on how that decoder is realized under finite precision."},"_bibtex":{"value":"@inproceedings{

===== FlexBI: Regaining Execution Flexibility for Batch-Invariant LLM Inference | ICLR 2027 Conference Submission | 2026-09-18 | forum rGmv0X20Oj
KW: ['batch-invariant inference', 'deterministic inference', 'large language model inference', 'kernel scheduling']
ABSTRACT: Batch-invariant (BI) inference preserves bitwise-identical results for each request regardless of its surrounding batch.
Existing BI implementations couple this numerical guarantee to fixed physical schedules, limiting their ability to exploit changing concurrency and prefix sharing. FlexBI regains execution flexibility by separating a fixed request-local numerical contract from adaptive physical scheduling. Flextile regains dynamic GEMM output tiling by keeping each output's reduction trace invariant across tile changes.
Flexload uses partition-invariant sharing to share identical physical key-value (KV) page loads while preserving each query's logical reduction. In online serving across two models and two datasets, FlexBI  delivers 25--33\% higher output throughput and 16--32\% lower P99 time to first token than same-engine BI in vLLM and SGLang.

===== God Does Not Play Dice: Enforcing Batch Invariance in Agentic Kernel Generation | ICLR 2027 Conference Submission | 2026-09-17 | forum hvO7ZzQiqG
KW: ['LLM Agents', 'GPU Kernel Optimization', 'Code Generation', 'Batch Invariance', 'Reproducibility']
ABSTRACT: Large language model (LLM) serving systems dynamically batch user requests for GPU execution, so the same request may be processed alongside different requests across runs. If the GPU kernels lack batch invariance (BI), this changing batch context can alter the numerical output for an unchanged input, undermining reproducibility. Existing kernel generation agents focus on correctness and efficiency but overlook BI. We find 19 confirmed BI violations among 83 batch-applicable released artifacts. To address this limitation, we propose BIEvolve, which combines contract-guided static dependency analysis with dynamic validation of bitwise consistency across batch contexts. BIEvolve is designed as a plug-in component for general kernel agents, allowing their original optimization capabilities to be reused while adding BI enforcement. We integrate it as successive acceptance gates in the optimization loop, rejecting structurally risky or dynamically non-invariant candidates before performance benchmarking and returning feedback to the agent. Experiments across three agent frameworks under baseline and BI-aware generation on real-world LLM serving tasks show that BIEvolve improves the BI pass rate from 67.6% to 91.9% while retaining 91.8% of the baseline geometric mean speedup. These results demonstrate that BIEvolve can be incorporated into kernel optimization by agents as an additional reliability objective alongside correctness and speed. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/BIEvolve-50F0/.

===== Quantization Modulates Batch-Context Non-Determinism in Greedy LLM Inference | ICLR 2027 Conference Submission | 2026-09-19 | forum 9kskCmPMqd
KW: ['quantization', 'LLM inference', 'reproducibility', 'non-determinism', 'FP8', 'GPTQ', 'batch invariance', 'evaluation', 'decoding']
ABSTRACT: Quantization reduces the memory and compute cost of LLM inference, and requests are usually batched to serve many of them at once. However, recent studies have shown that batching causes non-determinism in LLM inference despite the use of greedy decoding. We study whether quantization changes this batch-context non-determinism, holding prompts, decoding settings and checkpoints fixed. For that we evaluate primarily Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across seven benchmarks and six serving contexts using BF16, GPTQ, FP8 weight-and-activation quantization, and FP8 KV-cache quantization. We observe answer disagreement across every pair of our serving contexts. FP8 weight-and-activation quantization roughly doubles how often an example changes its answer, from 8.7% to 17.2% for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and from 13.9% to 25.3% for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, while weight-only GPTQ stays close to BF16. Quantizing only the KV cache also raises the rate, and smaller evaluations on five further models show the same pattern. We trace the cause to the order in which floating-point reductions are carried out, which depends on batch composition. When we use batch-invariant kernels, the non-determinism effect vanishes for BF16 and FP8 at a throughput loss, but it remains for GPTQ.

===== Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference via Integer-Only Arithmetic | ODI 2026 Poster | 2026-08-14 | forum yCJPh9NkW1
KW: ['deterministic inference', 'integer-only arithmetic', 'on-device inference', 'quantization', 'reproducibility']
ABSTRACT: LLM inference is nondeterministic even at temperature 0. Floating-point addition is not associative, so the logits depend on the reduction order of whichever kernel runs, and batch shape, prefill vs. decode, library heuristics, and hardware all change which kernel that is. Batch-invariant kernels address this by pinning a single order, which scopes determinism to those kernels on that platform. Integer addition, by contrast, is associative: every reduction order yields the same bits. DetLLM runs the entire forward pass of Qwen3-0.6B (every matmul, softmax, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, and rotary embedding) in exact integer arithmetic, with no floating-point operation anywhere between input ids and int32 logits. Nine 512-token greedy generations spanning NVIDIA A100 and H100 GPUs and AMD, Intel, and Apple CPUs (four vendors, three instruction sets) produce one identical chained hash over all 512 logit vectors. Nine matched fp16 runs produce nine distinct hashes, and every pair disagrees from the first token. One int8 artifact serves every device, server GPU or laptop CPU, with nothing tuned per platform. WikiText2 perplexity comes out to 20.72 vs. 20.95 for fp16. Compiled, CUDA-graphed integer decode reaches 106 tok/s at batch 1 on an A100, 3.6× an eager fp16 baseline; we did not measure a comparably optimized fp16 baseline, and prefill runs at 0.13× fp16.

TITLE: [ROCm][Kernel] Extend skinny gemm N=5 to N=8 cases on GFX12 (RDNA4) using  SWMMAC optimization

## Purpose

This PR adds an optimized ROCm GFX12 (RDNA4) SWMMAC-based skinny GEMM path.

The new path targets serving workloads with low max concurrency, matching the benchmarked decode GEMM range of N=5-8. The implementation uses sparse wave matrix multiply-accumulate instructions on GFX12 (RDNA4) to improve throughput for these skinny GEMM cases, while keeping the existing fallback path for unsupported cases.

Skinny GEMMs can be important for ROCm/GFX12 (RDNA4) serving performance, which is often used in local or small-scale serving setups. In these deployments, the server is expected to handle single users, or a small number of users with a relatively lower request rate, so the active decode batch can remain small instead of being filled to a large batch size.

This optimization follows the same general direction described in the Hugging Face technical blog, [*Creating custom kernels for the AMD MI300*](https://huggingface.co/blog/mi300kernels). The blog discusses custom kernels for AMD MI300X vLLM serving and describes a skinny GEMM optimization for inputs with 8 or fewer rows.

The key idea is to map each logical skinny A row into two adjacent SWMMAC sparse rows. The first sparse row selects one set of 16-bit pairs from `A[n, :]`, and the second sparse row selects the complementary pairs from the same logical row. Both sparse rows multiply with the same normal `B[32 x 16]` fragment, producing two partial accumulator rows. The epilogue then adds the adjacent partial rows back together to recover the final logical output row. This interleaved sparse-row layout lets the kernel use the SWMMAC instruction shape more effectively for N=5-8 instead of leaving the skinny rows underfilled.

A related optimization direction is also being explored in IREE: [*[AMDG

The kernel compiles for gfx11 and gfx12, and everything here was measured on gfx1151, so **every commit gates itself to gfx115x** -- the tuning and the routing alike. Off gfx115x the kernel runs exactly as it does today: the K * N bound stays at 1.2x LDS, the chunked path never launches, every tuple takes the checked K loop, the zero point keeps its own pass over the unpacked values, and the dispatch keeps its current tuples. | Metric | Before | After | Change |

# LayerCast: Summary from the arXiv HTML (2506.09501v2)

**Design (BF16 weights, FP32 compute)**
- LayerCast is described as "a hybrid precision approach that balances computational stability with memory efficiency."
- It works in three steps:
  1. The model loads in FP32.
  2. All linear-layer weights and biases are cast to BF16 for storage before inference.
  3. During inference, each weight is upcast back to FP32 "just-in-time for matrix multiplication, one at a time."
- The result is that "all computations occur in full FP32 precision while storing weights in memory-efficient 16-bit formats."
- The authors argue the BF16→FP32 cast "is a deterministic operation that introduces no additional variance."
- They release it as a vLLM patch that needs only a few lines of code change.

**Memory and speed overhead**
- **Full FP32 vs BF16:** FP32 "doubles the memory usage and inference time compared to BF16."
- **LayerCast vs full FP32:** "memory usage is reduced by 34%," which the authors flag as important for the KV cache in long contexts.
- **LayerCast vs BF16:** No measured memory or speed numbers are given. The paper only says the footprint "remains closer to that of 16-bit models."
- **LayerCast speed:** No latency or throughput figures for LayerCast are reported in this content.

**Reproducibility gains**
- **Divergence rates (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, MATH500):**
  - LayerCast: "divergence rates below 3.4%"
  - FP32: "only 2.2% of the samples diverging"
  - BF16: "over 90% of examples showing divergence"
- **Std@Acc for R1-Qwen-7B (Table 25), LayerCast / FP32 / BF16:**

  | Benchmark | LayerCast | FP32 | BF16 |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | AIME'24 | 0 | 0 | 0.0544 |
  | MATH500 | 0.0011 | 0.0013 | 0.0114 |
  | LCB-Easy | 0.0049 | 0.0022 | 0.0169 |
  | LCB-Medium | 0.0043 | 0.0025 | 0.0176 |
  | LCB-Hard | 0.0044 | 0.0044 | 0.0066 |

- **R1-Llama-8B on AIME'24 (12 configurations):** LayerCast and FP32 both score 36.67% in every configuration, i.e. 0% Std@Acc. BF16 shows 5.87% Std@Acc on A100 and 3.44% on L40S.
- **For context:** in BF16, R1-Qwen-7B on AIME'24 shows "up to 9% variation in accuracy and 9,000 tokens difference" in response length.

**Speculative decoding**
- The content does not mention it.

**Venue**
- NeurIPS 2025 is not mentioned anywhere in the provided text.
- The page shows only "arXiv:2506.09501v2 [cs.CL] 24 Oct 2025."

# TBIK Performance, Hardware, Batch Invariance, and Venue

## Performance overhead

**Kernel level (Tree-Based MatMul vs cuBLAS, not vLLM):**
- The test fixed K=6144 and N=2048 and varied M.
- At small M, the kernel is slower "due to the fixed block-size constraint."
- At larger batches it "achieves 63% of cuBLAS performance, reaching around 120 TFLOPS in BF16 compared to 190 TFLOPS for cuBLAS."
- The authors attribute the gap to extra temporary accumulators for tree reduction, which add I/O and arithmetic.
- In FP32, "both kernels achieve comparable performance."
- The authors say the implementation is unoptimized and mainly a proof of concept. They suggest block-size tuning and warp specialization as future improvements.

**End-to-end latency:**
- This was measured in **SGLang, not vLLM**. The model was Qwen3-8B on 4× NVIDIA H20 (TP=4) with NVLink, batch size 64, across varying input and output lengths.
- The BIO numbers use SGLang's own BIO implementation.
- BIO alone vs BF16: "about 10∼33% overhead."
- TBIK on top of BIO: "another 5∼30% relative to BF16."
- Total BIO+TBIK vs BF16: "ranging from 22% to 63%."
- Breakdown in Appendix H: "the MatMul kernel accounts for 2∼25% of the overhead." The All-Reduce "incurs a maximum of 10% overhead."
- The MatMul overhead stays limited because the row-parallel layers are only a small share of total compute.
- The All-Reduce cost is attributed to a lack of low-level optimization, not to the tree design itself.

## GPUs

- **Reproducibility tests:** NVIDIA L40S (main tables) and RTX PRO 6000 (appendix).
- **Latency tests:** NVIDIA H20.
- **RL tests:** 4× L40S (GRPO, Qwen3-1.7B on GSM8K, vLLM TP=4 vs FSDP TP=1).
- **Block-size grid search:** L40S.

## Batch invariance (invariance to M)

- TBIK is always used together with BIO.
- In vLLM, BIO handles the column-parallel layers, and Tree-Based MatMul handles the row-parallel layers (down_proj, o_proj), "to ensure both batch and TP invariance."
- The Tree MatMul uses fixed block sizes. For BF16 these are M=64, K=256, N=128, and each (m,n) output tile is reduced independently over K, which implies M-invariance.
- The paper does not explicitly claim standalone M-invariance for the tree kernel.
- In practice, BIO+TBIK gave 1 unique output across batch sizes 8/16/32 and TP 1/2/4/8.
- Caveat: chunked prefill had to be handled. It was disabled for RL, and the authors "set max_num_seqs=1" for Qwen3-32B with TP=2 on L40S.

## Speculative decoding and AMD

Neither is mentioned. All hardware tested is NVIDIA.

## Venue

No venue is stated. The page shows arXiv:2511.17826v2, dated 29 May 2026. It includes an "Impact Statement" section, which is consistent with an ICML-style format, but ICML 2026 is not confirmed anywhere in the text.

- In vLLM, BIO handles the column-parallel layers, and Tree-Based MatMul handles the row-parallel layers (down_proj, o_proj), "to ensure both batch and TP invariance."
- The Tree MatMul uses fixed block sizes. For BF16 these are M=64, K=256, N=128, and each (m,n) output tile is reduced independently over K, which implies M-invariance.
- The paper does not explicitly claim standalone M-invariance for the tree kernel.
- In practice, BIO+TBIK gave 1 unique output across batch sizes 8/16/32 and TP 1/2/4/8.
- Caveat: chunked prefill had to be handled. It was disabled for RL, and the authors "set max_num_seqs=1" for Qwen3-32B with TP=2 on L40S.

## Speculative decoding and AMD

Neither is mentioned. All hardware tested is NVIDIA.

## Venue

No venue is stated. The page shows arXiv:2511.17826v2, dated 29 May 2026. It includes an "Impact Statement" section, which is consistent with an ICML-style format, but ICML 2026 is not confirmed anywhere in the text.

content.content:
**Date and authors**
- The post was published July 9, 2025.
- It is credited to Rémi Ouazan Reboul (ror) and seungrok jung (seungrokj), with the AMD organization listed.
- The author (ror) posted a reply in the comments dated Jan 26.

**Skinny GEMM design (MI300X, FP8, Llama 3.1 405B)**

*Split-K*
- Yes, the kernel uses split-K. The shared K axis is divided into sub-GEMMs that run at the same time, which multiplies the number of CUs in use.
- The partial results are then added together afterward.
- The authors say this pays off "as long as K is large and the original GEMM uses less than 50% of the GPU."

*How rows are packed into MFMA*
- For FP8 there are only two dense instructions, `16x16x32` and `32x32x16`, plus one sparse `16x16x64`.
- With 8 rows, the dense path would need 8 rows of padding.
- Instead, the 8 dense rows are placed into a 16-row operand with 4:2 sparsity, so the sparse instruction applies.
- The benefit is depth: "the sparse instruction has twice the depth" for the same number of cycles (K=64 vs K=32).
- The authors say this speeds up "any input with 8 or less rows."

*Warp specialization*
- Producer warps load data from VRAM into shared-memory buffers, and consumer warps compute from those buffers.
- The two sides coordinate through a queue in shared memory. The author describes it in a comment as an "int16 variable in the shared memory (a semaphore)."
- The split is "typically 8 or 10" producers to "something like 2 or 3" consumers.
- The input and the weights have separate producers, with more assigned to the weights.
- The MI300X "has no warp-level barriers," which required inline ASM workarounds.

*Per-row arithmetic*
- The post does not describe any per-row arithmetic.

**Measured speedups**
- The baseline is Torch, which binds "a highly optimized GEMM taken from AMD's linear algebra library." hipBLASLt is never named as the measured baseline.
- Measurements used 500 warmup iterations, 2000 profiling iterations, CUDA graph, and multiple weights to avoid cache hits.

| Projection | N × K | M=1 | M=8 | M=16 | M=32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| QKV | 2304 × 16384 | 127.84% (14.938→11.685 μs) | 132.07% | 120.02% | 98.80% (slower) |
| Gate/Up | 13312 × 16384 | 141.88% (77.636→54.717 μs) | 137.15% | 125.45% | 118.30% |
| Down | 16384 × 6656 | 112.51% | 112.17% | 104.76% | 101.45% |

- The authors suggest Torch "probably pads everything to 16 rows."

**Different code paths or accumulation orders by row count**
- The sparse path applies only to small M (≤8). A commenter who read the code says "sparsity is only used for M = 8," but the author's reply to that question is collapsed and not shown on the page.
- Split-K reorders the summation, but the post never discusses this in terms of numerical consistency.
- Nothing is said about whether accumulation order varies with M.

**Determinism, batch invariance, speculative decoding**
- None of these are mentioned anywhere in the article or the visible comments.

toolu_01JGfv5Vzd1K7iqsd4XqUr4K.prompt: Quote verbatim any sentence mentioning deterministic inference, batch invariance, or bit-exact / identical output relative to non-speculative decoding, and say which speculative modes it applies to. Also note any AMD/ROCm support statements.

content.content:
## Determinism, batch invariance, and identical output

**Deterministic inference (UNO only)**
- In UNO's list of unsupported features: "strict thinking, and deterministic inference are not yet supported." Deterministic inference is not available with UNO, in either linear or tree mode.

**Distributionally identical output (DFLASH with a LiLiCorr draft checkpoint)**
- "Verify is unchanged, so outputs remain distributionally identical to the target model's and only acceptance length moves."
- "Verify stays exact." This is said of the optional `SGLANG_ENABLE_LILICORR_SAMPLING=1` path.

**Bit-for-bit output (LiLiCorr sampling toggle)**
- "Off by default; with it unset the captured body is `select` itself, so temperature-0 output is unchanged bit for bit."
- This compares LiLiCorr with and without the sampling flag. It is not a comparison against non-speculative decoding.

**Related statements (preserving the distribution, not exact equality)**
- Block verification uses a correction distribution "to preserve target sampling." This covers stochastic EAGLE, EAGLE3, and NEXTN.
- "Greedy requests keep their existing verification behavior."
- For DFlash, "Backends also differ in attention numerics," so acceptance rates measured on different backends should not be compared directly.

**Not found**
- Nothing on the page mentions batch invariance.
- No sentence claims bit-exact output matching non-speculative decoding for any mode.

## AMD/ROCm

- The only ROCm mention is in the block verification section. It applies to stochastic EAGLE/EAGLE3/NEXTN "on NVIDIA CUDA or AMD ROCm" and requires `--speculative-eagle-topk 1`.
- Some modes are tied to CUDA:
  - NGRAM "only supports CUDA."
  - UNO "requires CUDA with FA3."
- The page says nothing about ROCm for any other mode.

## Novelty check: making speculative decoding bit-exact against plain decoding by keeping kernels invariant to small M

Searched through 2026-10-08: arXiv API, OpenReview API, GitHub issues/PRs (vLLM, SGLang, ROCm/aiter, TensorRT-LLM, FlashInfer, thinking-machines-lab/batch_invariant_ops, llama.cpp, Megatron-LM) and blogs. Closeness to your idea is rated H (high), M (medium) or L (low).

### 1. Evidence that speculative decoding is not bitwise lossless, and its consequences

**Papers and docs**

- **omphalos #136 / #161** (2026-10-01/02), a hobby engine for the AMD RX 9060 XT (RDNA4, 0 stars). Mechanistically almost exactly your idea, unpublished.

- **NeMo-RL speculative rollouts paper** (2604.26779, Apr 2026): treats speculative decoding as lossless and has the trainer recompute logprobs.

**Batch-invariant modes in vLLM and SGLang**
- **vLLM `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT`.** Based on the Thinking Machines Lab work; tracker #27433 (2025-10) lists speculative decoding as "might be hard" and AMD as nice-to-have.
  - ROCm support is PR #52231 (2026-08-14, still open). Under batch invariance it turns the skinny GEMMs off and skips `ROCM_AITER_FA`; CI mirrors run on MI250, MI300 and MI355.
- **vLLM PR #52522** (2026-08-16, open), "Batch-invariant support for speculative decoding".
  - Scope is sampling and preemption recovery only; it checks invariance across concurrency and request order, not equality with plain decoding.
  - With batch invariance on, throughput drops 25% for EAGLE3, 5% for DFlash, 3% for DSpark. **M**
- **SGLang deterministic mode** (LMSYS blog, 2025-09-22): about 34% average overhead; does not mention speculative decoding.
  - Issue #13123 (2025-11) reports EAGLE3 is non-deterministic even with the flag on.
  - The speculative decoding docs make no bit-exact claim against plain decoding; deterministic mode is explicitly unsupported in the UNO speculative mode.

**SGLang work on the verify path**
- **PRs #35539 / #35541** (2026-08-19, closed / draft), from issue #35150.
  - Routes deterministic DSpark verify attention through the Triton decode kernel, treating the verify block as independent decode streams.
  - Verify attention becomes bitwise equal to sequential decode; differences in the GDN recurrent state remain. **H** for the attention half of your idea.
- **PR #42145** (2026-10-01, open): on SM120, GEMMs with M up to a cap (e.g. 16) go to a Triton tile that matches DeepGEMM bit for bit (no split-K, K ascending).
  - Rows are invariant for M 1–64 and beyond.
  - Deterministic decode goes from 17.98 to 27.66 tok/s, against 26.4 tok/s non-deterministic.
  - With DFlash in deterministic mode: 85.6 → 106.6 tok/s. **H** for the GEMM half (NVIDIA).

  - No split-K; each row is bit-identical alone or in batches of 2–16; slightly faster than cuBLAS at M=1.
  - ROCm builds are rejected. **H** (LM head only, CUDA only).
- **PR #33291**, Decode-Verify-Rollback (2026-08-02, open): fast draft, then a deterministic prefill-style verify, then rollback.
  - 1.58–2.65x faster than deterministic decode.
  - The reference output is the deterministic prefill-style verify pass, not plain decode. **M**
- **PR #42388** (2026-10-03, open): bit-exact replay of the GDN recurrent state for speculative verify. Exact against the default verify path, not against plain decoding. **L-M**

**Scheduling-based alternatives and formal approaches**
- **LLM-42** (2601.17768, Jan 2026, MSR/UW): fast decode, then verify windows of fixed shape (32–64 tokens) using the fact that kernels give the same result at any batch position for a fixed shape.

  - Reference output is the fixed verify shape; it is not prefill/decode-consistent and does not integrate with speculative decoding. **M**
- **MarginGate** (2605.30218, May 2026; ACL ARR and ICLR 2027 submissions): verifies only low-margin steps. Flips occur on 0.3–1.3% of steps; 100% determinism at 15–19% trigger rates; halves LLM-42's latency increment. **M**
- **CoRun** (2608.14376, Aug 2026): pads decode to one fixed shape (one CUDA graph, 256 slots) and runs prefill in isolation.
  - 15–324% higher throughput than batch-invariant kernels; decode step 32.6 ms vs 88.4 ms batch-invariant vs 19.4 ms default.
  - Reference is the padded shape. Implication for you: padding plain decode to M=k+1 is a trivial baseline you must beat. **M**
- **Vosti** (2609.38981, Sep 2026, Duke): formal specification covering prefill/decode and query-length invariance, with a Z3 checker for Triton kernels.
  - Matmul tiles depend only on N and K, not M.
  - Found failures in vLLM batch-invariant mode and SGLang deterministic mode, e.g. prefill vs decode mismatched on 192/384 Gemma3 pairs with vLLM's invariant Triton backend.

- **Thinking Machines Lab blog** (2025-09-10): a fixed split *size* for the KV cache (not a fixed number of splits) gives invariance to query count and chunking. One kernel config for all shapes is about 20% below cuBLAS; end to end 26 s → 55 s → 42 s.
- **vLLM M-bucketed tiles with BLOCK_K fixed per (N, K)**:
  - #53247 (merged 2026-08-24): about 3x faster decode kernels on RTX 4090D / H20.
  - #53649: −33.6% end-to-end latency on Blackwell.
  - #57586 (merged 2026-09-23): under `torch.compile`, the largest bucket's config was frozen into the graph, 3–6x slower; now uses breakable CUDA graphs so configs follow runtime M.
  - #60034 (2026-10-05, work in progress): Hopper 16-row tiles for M ≤ 16; batch-invariant decode 184 → 307 tok/s vs 573 default.
  - These tables are CUDA-only; ROCm uses the default config, which likely explains your 2.5x tax on MI250. **M-H**
- **SGLang ROCm #39725 → #39789** (2026-09-16, open): split-K sized by K only with a sequential reduce, free BLOCK_M/N, fused batch-invariant RMSNorm, causal bound on prefill attention.
  - MI355X batch-1 decode tax 3.17x → 1.76x; on gfx942, split-K alone gave 1.15–1.51x. **H** for AMD, but still about a 1.7x tax and no speculative decoding.
- **FlexBI** (ICLR 2027 submission, Sep 2026): output tiling may change while each output's reduction trace stays fixed, plus KV page loads shared without changing any query's reduction. 25–33% more throughput than same-engine batch invariance in vLLM and SGLang. **M-H**
- **"Taming Bitwise Behavior in GPU Kernels with Tensor Core"** (2609.11356, Sep 2026): a descriptor of GEMM reduction order.
  - BLOCK_M/N/K are only speed knobs; the instruction's K depth and split-K change the bits.
  - A static bit-equivalence checker covers PTX and AMDGCN (gfx942) and can restrict autotuning to one equivalence class. A useful tool for certifying your kernels. **M**
- **vLLM #40179** (2026-04, closed): on ROCm, rocBLAS's Tensile backend picks tiling by M, causing prefix-caching mismatch; fixed by aligning M in the scheduler. **L-M**

### 4. Skinny GEMMs on AMD MI200/MI300 and M-invariance
**No source claims M-invariance for any of these.**

- **vLLM ROCm dispatch** (vLLM main, Oct 2026; may differ slightly from your 0.30 build):
  - gfx9, which includes gfx90a/MI250: `wvSplitK` handles 1 ≤ tokens ≤ 5. N=5 was added for speculative verify in #40687 (merged 2026-05-28, +14% decode on gfx1151).
  - `LLMM1` is used only for 1 token with an output size of 4 or 8 (practically never for LLM layers).
  - 6 or more tokens go to AITER's tuned GEMM or `F.linear` (hipBLASLt).
- **`wvSplitKrc`** (gfx950 only, 10–128 tokens) picks its K-shard split from the token count, so it is not M-invariant.
  - Its atomics made it nondeterministic run to run; a deterministic store-then-reduce path is now the default (#34304, merged 2026-03-10).
  - ROCm CI disabled skinny GEMMs to get determinism (#35152, #35049). PR #35183 (closed) notes that bitwise reproducibility matters for speculative verify — but that is run-to-run, not M-invariance.
- **My own reading of the code, not a published claim:**
  - In `wvSplitK`, each output's K-reduction does not depend on N, YTILE, UNRL or the LDS variant: per-lane strided `v_dot2` or MFMA-4x4x4-bf16 accumulation per row, then a fixed DPP butterfly.
  - So decode and verify with up to 4 drafts are probably already row-identical on MI250. A quick bitwise test is worth running.
  - If so, your divergence likely comes from verifies with 6+ tokens falling back to hipBLASLt, from attention, or from norms.
  - At TP=2 the all-reduce is a single commutative add per element, so it is likely invariant unless precision or quantization (e.g. QuickReduce) changes with message size.
- **AITER tuned GEMM:** picks a per-M tuned solution, padding M to the nearest tuned row.
  - Its FlyDSL bf16 kernels with split-K=4 are nondeterministic and disagree with PyTorch on 37–50% of outputs (aiter #6114, 2026-10-03).
  - Split-K partial sums are reduced in BF16 (aiter #5976).
- **HF blog "Creating custom kernels for the AMD MI300"** (2025-07-09): MI300X FP8 skinny GEMM for M ≤ 8 using a sparse-MFMA trick plus split-K; 12–42% faster than torch at M=1–16. Determinism is not discussed, and the M ≤ 8 sparse path changes the arithmetic across M.
- **vLLM #45559** (RDNA4, N=5–8): splits each row into two sparse rows summed in the epilogue, so its arithmetic differs from the N ≤ 4 path.
- No study of the "verify tax" on CDNA was found.

### Verdict
The phenomenon, its root cause (the verify pass at M=k+1 vs decode at M=1) and every kernel ingredient of your fix are already documented: K-order fixed across M buckets, split-K sized by K, a fixed KV split size, verify attention run as decode, and a decode-only invariant bucket (vLLM RFC #54506, ICLR'27 "Lossless, Yet Not Identical", 2609.15504, vLLM #53247/#60034, SGLang #42145/#42867/#39789/#35541, 2609.25624, FlexBI, Vosti), and omphalos has already done it end to end on consumer AMD at +0.2% cost. What appears unclaimed is a scoped "verify-invariance" mode in a production engine on AMD CDNA (MI250/MI300, with TP) that makes all lossless speculative methods (MTP, EAGLE/DFlash, n-gram, suffix) bit-exact against plain decoding at near-zero cost. That would include systematic divergence measurements and the RL/evaluation consequences, plus the finding that the same invariant skinny-GEMM family also removes the CDNA verify tax; vLLM RFC #54506 explicitly asks for this without a design. Expect fast overlap from open PRs (vLLM #52522, #54506, #60034, #52231; SGLang #42145, #42867, #39789) and the ICLR'27 submissions, so the contribution must rest on the CDNA kernel design, near-zero-cost evidence against padding and full batch-invariance baselines, and the consequences — not on the concept.

### 3. Cheaper-than-full batch invariance, especially on AMD
- **Thinking Machines Lab blog** (2025-09-10): a fixed split *size* for the KV cache (not a fixed number of splits) gives invariance to query count and chunking. One kernel config for all shapes is about 20% below cuBLAS; end to end 26 s → 55 s → 42 s.
- **vLLM M-bucketed tiles with BLOCK_K fixed per (N, K)**:
  - #53247 (merged 2026-08-24): about 3x faster decode kernels on RTX 4090D / H20.
  - #53649: −33.6% end-to-end latency on Blackwell.
  - #57586 (merged 2026-09-23): under `torch.compile`, the largest bucket's config was frozen into the graph, 3–6x slower; now uses breakable CUDA graphs so configs follow runtime M.
  - #60034 (2026-10-05, work in progress): Hopper 16-row tiles for M ≤ 16; batch-invariant decode 184 → 307 tok/s vs 573 default.

### 4. Skinny GEMMs on AMD MI200/MI300 and M-invariance
**No source claims M-invariance for any of these.**

- **vLLM ROCm dispatch** (vLLM main, Oct 2026; may differ slightly from your 0.30 build):
  - gfx9, which includes gfx90a/MI250: `wvSplitK` handles 1 ≤ tokens ≤ 5. N=5 was added for speculative verify in #40687 (merged 2026-05-28, +14% decode on gfx1151).
  - `LLMM1` is used only for 1 token with an output size of 4 or 8 (practically never for LLM layers).
  - 6 or more tokens go to AITER's tuned GEMM or `F.linear` (hipBLASLt).
- **`wvSplitKrc`** (gfx950 only, 10–128 tokens) picks its K-shard split from the token count, so it is not M-invariant.
  - Its atomics made it nondeterministic run to run; a deterministic store-then-reduce path is now the default (#34304, merged 2026-03-10).
  - ROCm CI disabled skinny GEMMs to get determinism (#35152, #35049). PR #35183 (closed) notes that bitwise reproducibility matters for speculative verify — but that is run-to-run, not M-invariance.
- **My own reading of the code, not a published claim:**
  - In `wvSplitK`, each output's K-reduction does not depend on N, YTILE, UNRL or the LDS variant: per-lane strided `v_dot2` or MFMA-4x4x4-bf16 accumulation per row, then a fixed DPP butterfly.
  - So decode and verify with up to 4 drafts are probably already row-identical on MI250. A quick bitwise test is worth running.
  - If so, your divergence likely comes from verifies with 6+ tokens falling back to hipBLASLt, from attention, or from norms.
  - At TP=2 the all-reduce is a single commutative add per element, so it is likely invariant unless precision or quantization (e.g. QuickReduce) changes with message size.
- **AITER tuned GEMM:** picks a per-M tuned solution, padding M to the nearest tuned row.
  - Its FlyDSL bf16 kernels with split-K=4 are nondeterministic and disagree with PyTorch on 37–50% of outputs (aiter #6114, 2026-10-03).
  - Split-K partial sums are reduced in BF16 (aiter #5976).
- **HF blog "Creating custom kernels for the AMD MI300"** (2025-07-09): MI300X FP8 skinny GEMM for M ≤ 8 using a sparse-MFMA trick plus split-K; 12–42% faster than torch at M=1–16. Determinism is not discussed, and the M ≤ 8 sparse path changes the arithmetic across M.
- **vLLM #45559** (RDNA4, N=5–8): splits each row into two sparse rows summed in the epilogue, so its arithmetic differs from the N ≤ 4 path.
- No study of the "verify tax" on CDNA was found.

### Verdict
The phenomenon, its root cause (the verify pass at M=k+1 vs decode at M=1) and every kernel ingredient of your fix are already documented: K-order fixed across M buckets, split-K sized by K, a fixed KV split size, verify attention run as decode, and a decode-only invariant bucket (vLLM RFC #54506, ICLR'27 "Lossless, Yet Not Identical", 2609.15504, vLLM #53247/#60034, SGLang #42145/#42867/#39789/#35541, 2609.25624, FlexBI, Vosti), and omphalos has already done it end to end on consumer AMD at +0.2% cost. What appears unclaimed is a scoped "verify-invariance" mode in a production engine on AMD CDNA (MI250/MI300, with TP) that makes all lossless speculative methods (MTP, EAGLE/DFlash, n-gram, suffix) bit-exact against plain decoding at near-zero cost. That would include systematic divergence measurements and the RL/evaluation consequences, plus the finding that the same invariant skinny-GEMM family also removes the CDNA verify tax; vLLM RFC #54506 explicitly asks for this without a design. Expect fast overlap from open PRs (vLLM #52522, #54506, #60034, #52231; SGLang #42145, #42867, #39789) and the ICLR'27 submissions, so the contribution must rest on the CDNA kernel design, near-zero-cost evidence against padding and full batch-invariance baselines, and the consequences — not on the concept.
